# THE LIFE of Apollonius, the Poet of the *Argonautica*. <note>original: "ΓΕΝΟΣ" (Genos). This was a standard biographical "Life" or "Lineage" prefixed to ancient texts to provide context about the author.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Apollonius, the poet of the *Argonautica* <term>Argonautica</term> <note>The epic poem recounting the voyage of the ship *Argo* to retrieve the Golden Fleece.</note>, was an Alexandrian by birth, the son of Silleus—though some say his father was Illeus. He belonged to the Ptolemais tribe and lived during the time of the Ptolemies. He was a student of Callimachus <note>A famous scholar-poet and head of the Library of Alexandria.</note>; at first, he studied alongside Callimachus, his own teacher, but later he turned to the composition of poetry. It is said that while he was still a youth, he gave a public recitation of the *Argonautica* and was condemned <note>Or "poorly received."</note>. Unable to bear the shame before his fellow citizens, the disgrace, and the slander of other poets, he left his homeland and moved to Rhodes. There, he refined and corrected his work through diligent labor. He then gave another recitation and won great acclaim. For this reason, he identifies himself as "the Rhodian" in his poems. He taught with great distinction in Rhodes and was granted citizenship and honors by the Rhodians. This concludes the account of his life. As for the plot <note>original: "ὑπόθεσις" (hypothesis). A summary of the mythological background or "argument" of the story.</note> of the *Argonautica*, it follows this manner:

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Tyro, the daughter of Salmoneus, gave birth to Neleus and Pelias by Poseidon. Later, she married Cretheus, her father’s brother, and bore him Aeson, Pheres, and Amythaon. From Aeson came Jason; from Pheres, Admetus; and from Amythaon, Melampus. Jason was sent to Chiron <note>The wise centaur who acted as a tutor to many Greek heroes.</note> to be raised, where he also learned the art of medicine. Meanwhile, his father Aeson had left the kingdom to his own brother, Pelias, commanding him to rule over Thessaly until Jason reached adulthood. Pelias had received an oracle from Apollo to beware of the "one-sandaled man" <term>monopedilon</term> <note>original: "μονοπέδιλον". A person wearing only one shoe, which served as a prophetic sign of Pelias's downfall.</note> who would come to him, for he would meet his death because of him. 

When Jason was grown, he went to his father’s brothers to learn about his father’s kingdom or to claim it for himself. While at the Anaurus river (which is in Thessaly) and wishing to cross, he found Hera disguised as an old woman. She wished to be carried across but was afraid of the rushing water. Jason took her upon his shoulders and brought her safely across, but in the middle of the river, he lost one sandal in the mud. He then proceeded to the city with only one sandal. He found a public festival and a sacrifice being offered to the gods by Pelias. When Pelias saw Jason with only one sandal, he remembered the oracle. Being cautious about killing him outright, he assigned him a labor <note>original: "ἆθλον" (athlon), the same word used for the Labors of Hercules.</note>, saying: "Go to Scythia and bring back the Golden Fleece, and then you shall receive your father’s kingdom." He commanded this not because he desired the golden fleece <note>original: "κωδίου" (kōdiou), meaning a fleece or sheepskin.</note>, but because he thought...

...it was foretold to him in the marketplace that he would either be destroyed by someone or perish in a shipwreck at sea. The matter regarding the Golden Fleece <term>Golden Fleece</term> <note>The fleece of the winged ram, Chrysomallos, which became the object of Jason's quest.</note> is as follows:

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Athamas was the son of Aeolus and the brother of Cretheus. Having previously had a wife named Nephele <note>Her name means "Cloud."</note>, he fathered two children by her, Phrixus and Helle. After Nephele died, he took a second wife, Ino. She plotted against Nephele’s children and persuaded the local women to roast the seeds <note>original: "φρύγειν τὰ σπέρματα" (phrygein ta spermata). By roasting the grain before sowing, Ino ensured it would not germinate, causing a man-made famine.</note>; thus, the earth, receiving the roasted seed, did not yield its annual fruits. Athamas then sent messengers to Delphi to inquire about the infertility of the land. Ino, however, bribed the messengers with gifts and instructed them to claim that the god <note>The Oracle of Apollo at Delphi.</note> had declared that Helle and Phrixus must be sacrificed if they wished for a release from the famine. Persuaded by this, Athamas brought Helle and Phrixus to the altar. But the gods, taking pity on them, snatched them away through the air by means of a golden-fleeced ram. While in flight, Helle was unable to hold on and fell into the sea which was named the Hellespont <note>Literally "The Sea of Helle."</note> after her. Phrixus, however, was delivered safely to the land of Colchis. There, he sacrificed the ram to Zeus the Protector of Fugitives <note>original: "Διὶ φυξίῳ" (Dii Phyxio). A title for Zeus as the god who aids those in flight or exile.</note> because he had escaped his stepmother’s plot. He married Chalciope, the daughter of Aeetes, the king of the Scythians. He fathered four sons with her—Argus, Cytisorus, Melas, and Phrontis—and eventually passed away there.

## Another Version of the Life of Apollonius.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Apollonius the poet was an Alexandrian by birth. His father was Silleus (or perhaps Illeus), and his mother was Rhode. He was a student of Callimachus while the latter was a grammarian in Alexandria. Having composed these poems <note>The *Argonautica*.</note>, he gave a public recitation. However, he failed miserably and, blushing with shame, he retired to Rhodes. There, he lived as a citizen and practiced the rhetorical speeches of the sophists <note>Professional teachers of rhetoric and philosophy.</note>; for this reason, they called him "The Rhodian." While living there, he polished and refined his poems, and after giving another recitation, he achieved great fame—so much so that he was granted Rhodian citizenship and various honors. Some say that he later returned to Alexandria and, after reciting his work there once more, attained the highest degree of success, such that he was deemed worthy of the libraries of the Museum <note>The Great Library of Alexandria, part of the *Musaeum* or "Institution of the Muses."</note> and was even buried alongside Callimachus himself.

The commentary <term>scholia</term> <note>Ancient explanatory notes written in the margins of manuscripts.</note> provided here is drawn from the works of Lucillus of Tarrha, Sophocles, and Theon.
Tarrha is a city in Crete, as Lopinos says in his *Philological Studies*.

"Beginning" <note>original: "Ἀρχόμενος" (Archomenos)</note>: the participle is formed from a "middle-passive" verb. Middle-passive verbs are those that show both an action and a state of being acted upon <note>In Greek grammar, these are often "deponent" verbs, which have a passive form but an active meaning.</note>; for example: "I force," "I bestow," "I sacrifice." So too is the verb "I begin." In one sense, it means: "I am making a beginning from you"; for it is the custom to begin a poem with the gods, as in the phrase: "Let us begin from Zeus." In another sense, it means:

## ARGONAUTICA, BOOK ONE.

<margin>
...being under your power. Like one "inspired"; for poets are inspired in a manner very similar to those who are "mad" <note>The Greeks believed poetic inspiration was a form of "divine madness" or possession (enthousiasmos).</note>. Some also say that "beginning" <note>original: "ἀρχόμενος"</note> is used here instead of "having begun." Therefore, the meaning is: "having begun from you, I shall commemorate the glorious deeds of the Argonauts." The *Argo*: the...

**STARTING FROM YOU, O PHOEBUS <note>A title for Apollo, the god of music, poetry, and prophecy.</note>, I SHALL RECALL THE FAMOUS DEEDS OF MEN BORN LONG AGO, WHO, THROUGH THE MOUTH OF THE SEA AND BETWEEN THE DARK ROCKS <note>Known as the Symplegades, these were clashing islands that crushed ships attempting to enter the Black Sea.</note>, AT THE COMMAND OF KING PELIAS, DROVE THE WELL-BENCHED ARGO IN PURSUIT OF THE GOLDEN FLEECE. FOR PELIAS HAD HEARD SUCH A PROPHECY: THAT A HATEFUL FATE AWAITED HIM HEREAFTER—TO BE OVERTHROWN BY THE SCHEMES OF THAT MAN WHOM HE SHOULD SEE COMING FROM THE COMMON PEOPLE WEARING ONLY ONE SANDAL. AND NOT LONG AFTER, IN ACCORDANCE WITH YOUR PATH, JASON, AS YOU WERE CROSSING THE STREAMS OF THE WINTRY ANAURUS ON FOOT, YOU SAVED ONE SANDAL FROM THE MUD, BUT THE OTHER YOU LEFT BEHIND THERE, HELD FAST BY THE RUSHING WATERS.**

---

...Apollonius calls the ship *Argo* after Argus, the man who built it. However, the historian Pherecydes says it was named after Argus, the son of Phrixus. They say this was the first "long ship" <note>A galley or warship, as opposed to a round merchant vessel.</note> ever made. Others say that Danaus, while being pursued by Aegyptus, was the first to build one, which is why it was called the *Danais*. "Well-benched" means having good seats for the rowers. "For such a prophecy": the word "such" <note>original: "τοίην" (toien)</note> is used as a "responsive" word, showing a comparison or likeness in parables—such as: "as is the generation of leaves, *such* is that of men." It can also be used referentially, or to express wonder. "Anaurus" is what he calls the torrent; for rivers that are formed from rainwater are called by this name.

"Mouths of the river" <note>original: "Προχοῇσι" (Prochoēsi)</note>: the places where the rivers meet the sea are called "mouths"; as in Homer: "as when at the mouths." "Of Pelasgian Hera": in the Homeric style, he called Hera "Pelasgian" after the region of Thessaly. He distinguishes this from the Peloponnese, which he calls "Achaean Argos." [The author] speaks of the Thessalian Larissa <note>A major city in the region of Thessaly.</note>: it was founded by **Acrisius** and named after Larissa, daughter of Pelasgus, as **Hellanicus** <note>An early Greek historian.</note> says. He says there are three cities named Larissa: the most ancient is the "Argive" one, which is an acropolis. The second is in the Pelasgian region of Thessaly, which the younger [Homer] calls Larissa, near Gyrton; this is the one **Apollonius** mentions now. There is also a third near Troy, which **Homer** remembers as the "tribes of the Pelasgians." Regarding **Polyphemus**, Apollonius calls him the son of Elatus, but **Isocrates** and **Euphorion** call him the son of Poseidon. The **Lapiths** <note>A legendary people of Thessaly, famous for their battle against the Centaurs.</note> were named after Lapithes, the son of Apollo and the nymph Stilbe. "Nor indeed Iphiclus": Iphiclus was the son of Phylacus and Clymene, daughter of Minyas. **Hesiod** says of him that he could run across the tips of ripened grain <note>A common mythological trope for extreme speed.</note>; but **Demaratus** says he could run upon the sea. It is worth noting that both Hesiod and **Pherecydes** say that Iphiclus sailed with the Argonauts. Pherae was named after Pheres, the son of Kretheus and father of Admetus. "Rich in sheep" <note>original: "Eurrenessi"</note> is used instead of "possessing many flocks." Mount Chalcodonion is situated above the Amphrysian territory. "Nor did they remain at Alope": this is a city in Thessaly or Magnesia. "Rich in grain-fields" <note>original: "Polyleioi"</note> comes either from "leion" (a crop-bearing plain) or from "leia" (plunder), which is the better interpretation; for the text says they were "skilled in deceits," implying they were sleepless, clever, and enduring in toil. Aethalides is a proper name, though it follows the form of a patronymic <note>A name derived from a father or ancestor.</note>. "Amphrysus": some write this with a "b" <note>Amphrysos vs. Ambrusos</note>, as **Dionysius** does. It is a river in Thessaly. The accent is placed on the third-to-last syllable, as noted in the universal rules of grammar.

She had requested this from him, along with invulnerability. He even challenged Apollo and was defeated. This Caeneus commanded those passing by to swear by his spear; hence the proverb "the spear of Caeneus" <note>Used to describe someone who places their trust in weapons or brute force rather than the gods.</note>. **Near the Xynian lake:** Xynias is a lake in Thessaly. Some say it is a city situated near the Boebeid lake, and the poet called the area "Xynian" after the city. It is located in Phthia, to which the city belongs. Others say it is called "Xynian" <note>original: "ξυνιάδα" (Xyniada)</note> because of the word *xynon*, meaning "common" <note>original: "κοινόν" (koinon)</note>, because this lake was common territory to both Thessaly and Boeotia. **Dolopian Ctimene:** Ctimene is a city in Thessaly. He called the region "Dolopian" because the Dolopes are a tribe of Thessaly. As Homer says: "And I dwelt at the edge of Phthia, ruling over the Dolopes." <note>Homer, *Iliad* 9.484</note> **From Oroes:** Oroes is a city in Lokris. From Oroes comes the term *Eleion* <note>original: "ἠλεῖον". This likely refers to a geographical designation or a variant reading for the people of the region</note>. Homer says: "They who inhabited Kynos and Oroes and Kalliaros." <note>Homer, *Iliad* 2.531</note> Patroclus was the son of Menoetius and Sthenele. **And mighty Eribotes:** The word "mighty" <note>original: "ἀλκήεις" (alkēeis)</note> means strong. It is a derivative form from the word for "strength" <note>original: "ἀλκή" (alkē)</note>, just as the word for "voiced" <note>original: "φωνήεις" (phōnēeis)</note> is formed from "voice" <note>original: "φωνή" (phōnē)</note>. **Herodorus** in his *History of the Argonauts* calls him Eurybates and says he is the son of Teleon. The sons of Actor were Menoetius and Irus. Of these, Patroclus was the son of Menoetius, and Eurytion was the son of Irus.

"So it is not for humans": the sense is, there is no greater evil that a human fails to encounter. The word is spelled with an 'a'—*apautrein* <note>original: "ἀπαυρεῖν" (to take away/attain)</note>—meaning that no great evil is far from humans so as not to reach them, which means to "happen upon" or "attain." "But Theseus [did not surpass] all": Theseus and Peirithous—the former a descendant of Zeus, the latter of Poseidon—were heroes whose deeds were made to rival one another. Theseus, having fallen in love with Helen, had Peirithous assisting him in her abduction. But Peirithous, wishing to abduct Persephone <note>the Queen of the Underworld</note>, necessitated that Theseus follow him in return. And so, having descended into the realm of Hades through the entrance at Taenarum and having sat there upon a certain "Seat of Forgetfulness," they were unable to stand up again. 

However, Herakles, later descending to capture Cerberus <note>the three-headed hound of Hades</note>, rescued Theseus because he had not gone down of his own willing purpose; but he left Peirithous behind because he had descended by his own wicked choice. During this time, the Dioscuri <note>the twin brothers Castor and Pollux</note> also campaigned against Aphidna to rescue their sister Helen while Theseus was trapped in Hades; having sacked the city, they took captive Aethra, the mother of Theseus. "Taenarian": Pherecydes says in his eighth book that Elatus, the son of Icarus, married Erimyla, the daughter of Lamasiclus; from this union Taenarus was born, from whom both the city and the [region] are called Taenarum.

He speaks thus: "And the noble and wealthy Periclymenus, to whom Poseidon the Earth-Shaker gave all manner of gifts. For at one time indeed..."

Being a farmer and planting a vineyard, Ancaeus was very harsh toward his servants. One of the servants declared that the master would never taste the fruit of his harvest. When the grapes had finally ripened, Ancaeus joyfully held a sacrifice and ordered the servant to mix a cup of wine for him. As he was about to bring the cup to his mouth, he mockingly reminded the servant of his earlier words. The servant replied: "There is much between the cup and the edge of the lip." <note>This is the origin of the proverb "Many a slip 'twixt the cup and the lip"</note> While this was being said, a messenger arrived saying that a massive boar was ravaging the vineyard. Ancaeus threw down the drink, rushed out in a fury, and being struck by the boar, he died. Hence the proverb is used for those who find their expectations suddenly frustrated. Pherecydes also mentions this in his twentieth book.

The poets, having criticized him, gave him this description; "siphlos" means a blemish or defect. "From the Phocians": the Phocians were named after Phocus, the son of Aeacus. Pherecydes, when recounting the story of the abduction of Orithyia, says it was near the Thracian Sarpedonia, which is close to Mount Haemus. However, Choerilus says she was snatched by the springs of the Cephisus while she was gathering flowers.

"From Cecropia" <note>original: "Κεκροπίηθεν" (Kekropiethen)</note>: this refers to the Acropolis of Attica, which was formerly called Cecropia. "On the heights of their feet": this refers to the ankles and the talus bones. "Dark" <note>original: "Ἐρεμνὰς" (Eremnas)</note>: this is a shortened form of "shadowy" <note>original: "ἐρεβενὰς" (erebenas)</note>, meaning terrifying or specifically dark, from which we get the word "black." "Gloomy" <note>original: "Λυγαίοις" (Lygaiois)</note>: used figuratively for "dark"; the word for darkness <note>original: "λύγος" (lygos)</note> comes from the *lygos* plant, which is thick and bushy. "Scales" <note>original: "Φολίδεσιν" (Pholidesin)</note>: referring to the shimmering patterns or "embroidery" of the feathers. "From the top": that is, from the crown of the head. The meaning of the passage is clear.

meaning
he sends

He calls

> MOST AND THE BEST OF THEM BOASTED TO BE OF THE BLOOD
> OF MINYAS. THUS TOO HIS MOTHER ALCIMEDE BORE JASON HIMSELF,
> BORN FROM CLYMENE, DAUGHTER OF MINYAS.
> BUT WHEN EVERYTHING WAS PREPARED FOR THE SERVANTS—
> WHATEVER THINGS ARE MADE READY WITHIN SHIPS
> WHEN DUTY LEADS MEN TO SAIL OVER THE SEA—
> THEN THEY WENT THROUGH THE CITY TO THE SHIP, WHERE
> THE MAGNESIAN SHORES OF PAGASAE ARE FAMED. AND AROUND THEM
> A MULTITUDE OF PEOPLE RUNNING TOGETHER GATHERED. THEY SHONE
> LIKE BRIGHT STARS AMONG THE CLOUDS. AND THUS EACH ONE SPOKE,
> LOOKING AT THEM AS THEY RUSHED ALONG WITH THEIR WEAPONS:
> "LORD ZEUS! WHAT IS THE MIND OF PELIAS? TO WHAT PLACE DOES HE
> CAST OUT SUCH A THRONG OF HEROES FROM THE PANACHAEAN LAND?
> IN ONE DAY THEY WOULD DESTROY THE HALLS OF AEETES
> WITH DEADLY FIRE, IF HE DID NOT WILLINGLY HAND OVER THE FLEECE.
> BUT THE PATHS ARE NOT TO BE FLED; AND THE LABOR IS FRUITLESS FOR THOSE WHO GO."

this was the first region to be called Achaea, after Achaeus the son of Xuthus. "They would destroy with fire": they would burn it up, or war against it, or overturn it. "Halls" refers to the region or the land by way of synecdoche <note>term: synecdoche; a figure of speech where a part (the house) represents the whole (the country)</note>. "But the paths are not to be fled": meaning the journey is not one they can escape; for it is undertaken by necessity. Nor is the contest "fruitless" <note>original: "apraktos"</note>; for they will complete it easily, as if successfully. And "not to be fled" also suggests it is "not easy sailing" because of the dangers in between. "The labor is fruitless for those who go": namely, the danger inherent in the voyage. Or, the word "not" is applied to both clauses: so that it means "the paths are not to be fled, nor is the labor fruitless."

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Apollonius Rhodius's Argonautica, moving from the description of the heroes' departure to the specific lamentations of the women of Iolcus, particularly Jason’s mother, Alcimede. Regarding the phrase "on that very day may the house of Aeetes <note>The King of Colchis and keeper of the Golden Fleece</note> be ravaged by destructive fire," because he would not willingly hand over the fleece to them. Others explain the phrase "without success" <note>original: "aprēktos"</note> as: difficult to perform, hard to work, or hard to set right. "A heart-pleasing end to the journey" means "beneficial"; and the poet has fashioned this wonderfully well according to the different natures and speeches of both men and women. For since the nature of men is bolder, he assigns to them the accomplishment and the final result of future events. But for the women, since they are weaker, he has them offer prayers and supplications. For such

->VOICE—AN EVIL PORTENT—SO THAT HE MIGHT GIVE GRIEF..."<-

boasting of her life because of such a son. "Would that it had been for him" refers to the time before this labor <note>the quest for the Fleece</note> was imposed upon him. "Of evil [labors]" refers either to his own personal misfortunes or those destined to be fulfilled by the Argonauts. "Would that Phrixus also" <note>Phrixus and his sister Helle fled their stepmother on a golden ram; Helle fell into the sea, now called the Hellespont</note>: for it is said that when Helle fell, the ram spoke by the will of Zeus to encourage the agonizing Phrixus. It promised to save them and bring them to Scythia. This event was destined to become an evil for Alcimede herself, since her son was now journeying to that same place. Regarding the fact that the ram spoke, Hecataeus <note>an early Greek historian and geographer</note> also affirms it. However, some suggest that he actually sailed on a ship with a ram-shaped prow. Dionysius <note>likely Dionysius Scytobrachion, a mythographer</note> says in his second book that "Ram" <note>original: "Krios"</note> was actually the name of Phrixus’s tutor, who sailed with him to Colchis; he claims this is why the myths regarding the sacrifice of the ram were later invented there.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Argonautica, specifically focusing on the departure of the Argonauts and the profound grief it causes Jason's parents. It provides a linguistic and thematic analysis of the verses where Jason’s mother, Alcimede, and his father, Aeson, react to his leaving for the quest of the Golden Fleece.</meta>

"On the threshold" <note>original: *promolēsi*</note> refers to the exit of the noblemen; it is derived from "moving forward." From this, people also call the first foothills of mountains "promolai." "Stricken" <note>original: *bebolēmenē*</note> means damaged by grief or being despondent. "A sharp [pain] to each" is a metaphor transferred from the sense of touch, as found in Homer: "as when a sharp arrow holds a woman in labor." "Anguish" <note>original: *achos*</note> is a confusion of the soul intensified by grief. The general sense is clear from the words; or "they were grieving,"

<margin>Grant he might have perished.</margin>
<margin>"Pressed tight against the bed" <note>original: *en typas en lecheëssin*</note>: so excessively wrapped that all the limbs leave an impression through the tight wrapping. Homer says "wrapped tight in a cloak"; the term *en typas* is also used for the loins.</margin>

> **ALCIMEDE; AND LATER SHE WOULD PLACE MYRIAD PAINS.**
> **THUS THEY SPOKE AS THEY WENT TO THE THRESHOLD.**
> **AND NOW MANY MALE AND FEMALE SERVANTS GATHERED.**
> **BUT HIS MOTHER CLUNG AROUND HIM, STRICKEN. A SHARP**
> **ANGUISH ENTERED EACH WOMAN. AND WITH THEM HIS FATHER, UNDER DESTRUCTIVE OLD AGE,**
> **WRAPPED TIGHT AGAINST HIS BED, WAS WAILING.**
> **BUT THEN HE SOOTHED THEIR SORROWS**
> **GIVING THEM COURAGE. AND HE TOLD THE SERVANTS TO LIFT THE MARTIAL WEAPONS.**
> **AND THEY, DOWNCAST IN SILENCE, LIFTED THEM.**
> **BUT THE MOTHER, AS SHE FIRST THREW HER ARMS AROUND HIM,**
> **HELD HIM THUS, WEEPING INTENSELY. JUST LIKE A GIRL**
> **WHO, ALL ALONE, GLADLY FALLS UPON HER GREY-HAIRED NURSE.**

Stricken in appearance, just as his fate is perceived through his garments. "Downcast" <note>original: *katēpheas*</note> means shamed because of grief. The word "lifted" <note>original: *ēeironto*</note> is used in the passive voice instead of the active, or "poured over" <note>original: *epecheuato*</note> instead of "placed upon" or "threw upon." "More intensely" <note>original: *adinōteron*</note>: the form is similar to "blacker" <note>original: *melanteron*</note> or "more fat." For the poet used the comparative form instead of the simple form. "Just like a girl" <note>original: *ēyte kourē*</note>: the poet has constructed the simile in a way that seems inconsistent <note>The commentator notes it is unusual to compare a mother to a daughter and a son to a nurse</note>; for Jason is cast as the old nurse, and his mother as the young girl. But if one says he arranged these roles in reverse, we shall argue that Jason is suitably positioned—not according to his actual age, but according to his role in caring for his mother in her old age. For just as an old woman raises a girl, so a mother relies on her son when she is weakened by age. Indeed, old age and extreme youth are similar in their need for a caregiver. The figure of Pelias <note>The king who sent Jason on the dangerous quest</note> hangs over the mother like an exile. The word "solicitude" <note>original: *kēdemoneias*</note> is an expansion from "guardians"; this is how relatives by marriage and those who care for others are described. "In vain": This also refers to Alcimede; or perhaps that they are unrefined children.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Book 1 of the Argonautica. Having described the grief of Jason’s parents at his departure, the text now focuses on a specific simile comparing his mother, Alcimede, to a young girl suffering under a stepmother, while also providing philological notes on the vocabulary of mourning and wandering.</meta>

"A heavy life" <note>original: *bioton baryn*</note>. The word "being" <note>original: *ousa*</note> is omitted here. Being under a stepmother, she leads a miserable existence; for the term "life" <note>original: *biotos*</note> is used both for one's "span of life" (as it is used here) and for "wealth" or "livelihood." The terms *ēgēlazei* and *ēgēlaskei* <note>meaning to wander or linger</note> are used for the same concept. They signify a 

<margin>

and turning
about in the

<note>original: *ēlaskousi*</note>

To "burst out"
<note>original: *ekphlyxai*</note>.
Instead of

**SHE MOURNS. OR PERHAPS THERE ARE NO OTHER GUARDIANS LEFT.**
**BUT UNDER A STEPMOTHER, SHE DRAGS OUT A HEAVY LIFE.**
**AND LATELY SHE HAS BEEN STRUCK BY MANY INSULTS;**
**TO HER, AS SHE WAILS, HER HEART IS BOUND WITHIN BY RUIN.**
**NOR CAN SHE BURST OUT WITH AS MUCH LAMENTATION AS SHE DESIRES,**
**THUS ALCIMEDE WEPT CONTINUOUSLY, HOLDING HER OWN CHILD IN HER ARMS.**
**AND SHE SPOKE SUCH A WORD IN HER DISTRESS:**
**"WOULD THAT I HAD PERISHED <gloss>THROUGH THAT</gloss> ON THAT DAY WHEN I HEARD**
**WRETCHED THAT I AM, THE EVIL COMMAND OF KING PELIAS.**
**SO THAT I MIGHT HAVE IMMEDIATELY GIVEN UP MY SOUL AND FORGOTTEN MY CARES,**
**SO THAT YOU YOURSELF MIGHT HAVE BURIED ME WITH YOUR OWN DEAR HANDS,**
**MY CHILD. FOR THIS WAS THE ONLY LONGING LEFT TO ME**
**FROM YOU. BUT ALL OTHER REWARDS FOR YOUR REARING I HAVE LONG SINCE ENJOYED."**

We say that boiling cauldrons <note>original: *lebetas*</note> throw up water because of the heat. The term "to stretch out/gasp" <note>original: *orechthein*</note> is presented as a breath. It is a bellowing sound of an unarticulated voice. As Homer says: "at other times the oxen were bellowing <note>original: *orechtheon*</note>." But it should rather be understood here as "to groan" instead of "to be torn apart." Homer says: "gasping <note>original: *orechthōn*</note> with his heart in pains." It seems that the circumflexed form is written with an 'o' <note>omicron</note>, while the word with the accent on the third-to-last syllable is written with an 'ō' <note>omega</note>: *erechthō*. "So very much" <note>original: *hōde lian*</note>: entirely melted with grief. For it is impossible for a mother not to weep when her son is departing into such great danger. "Since not for the present" <note>original: *epei ou men pros to paron*</note>: not yet. "For there is no use in chilling lamentation."

The sanctuary of Themis in Athens. **Wailed** <note>original: *kinyreto*</note>: she lamented. Strictly speaking, *kinyresthai* is used of living beings; it is either derived from "moving the tail" <note>original: *kinein ten ouran*</note> while lowing, or according to Asios who found this etymology in Apollodorus, because a bull is called *Tauros* from "stretching the tail" <note>original: *teinein ten ouran*</note>. <meta>This page continues the text and commentary of Apollonius Rhodius's Argonautica, Book 1. Jason is responding to his mother Alcimede’s lament, attempting to comfort her as he prepares to lead the expedition for the Golden Fleece. The commentary (scholia) continues to draw parallels between Apollonius’s language and the foundational works of Homer, as well as the interpretations of the great librarian-scholar Aristarchus.</meta>

**But she bore** <note>original: *All' etiken*</note>: compared to the Homeric usage or the earlier "evil upon evil," it refers to "other sufferings." **You might gain** <note>original: *Aroio*</note>: he took. From this, some etymologize the word for "bear" <note>original: *arktos*</note> from "taking" and "benefiting" in war. The meaning of the passage is: "You have made evil on top of evil." **Though grieving** <note>original: *Aniazousa per*</note>: the conjunction *per* is often placed instead of "for" <note>original: *gar*</note> and "indeed" <note>original: *de*</note>. As in: "Not even if you are thus good" <note>original: *me d' outos agathos per eon*</note>. This is how Aristarchus <note>Aristarchus of Samothrace, the most influential scholar of the Library of Alexandria</note> explained it; for in the phrase "though being good," the *per* takes the meaning of "indeed," just like the word *de*.

<margin>
And here, then, 
the *per* is taken 
as "indeed." 
"Truly being 
good." And 
"whatever

is used for

BUT YOU NOW STAY HERE QUIETLY WITH YOUR SERVANTS
IN THE HOUSE. AND DO NOT BE AN ILL-OMENED BIRD <note>In antiquity, birds were primary sources of omens; here Jason asks his mother not to be a "bad luck charm" through her weeping</note> FOR THE SHIP.
YOUR KINSMEN AND SERVANTS WILL ACCOMPANY YOU THERE.
HE SPOKE, AND SET OUT TO GO FORWARD FROM THE HOUSE.

**Gave an oracle** <note>original: *Echre*</note>: used instead of "he prophesied" or "divined" concerning the voyage. **But then afterward**: in addition to what was said before regarding Athena and the prophecies, have courage further in the "aid of the heroes"—that is, their help. **But you now** <note>original: *Alla sy men*</note>: following the Homeric line: "But you, going into the house." **And do not be a bird**: again, following the Homeric: "Do not be an unlucky bird for me myself." **Will accompany you there**: "There" means to Colchis <note>the destination of the Argo</note> or to the harbor. "To accompany" <note>original: *homartein*</note> here means to follow, but elsewhere it means to meet together. **Kinsmen** <note>original: *etai*</note>: used instead of "companions" <note>original: *hetairoi*</note>. The word is a synonym, but it has been brought out in a shortened form. Homer was the first to use it, saying, "Brothers and kinsmen." Therefore, for the most part, it is expressed in the full form: "For I have no oared ships and companions." **Forward** <note>original: *Proterose*</note>: instead of "to the front." Homer says: "And then he went forward into the temple."

<meta>This page continues the commentary and text of Apollonius Rhodius’s Argonautica, Book 1. After comforting his mother, Jason departs for the ship. The commentator here explains the famous simile comparing Jason’s radiant appearance to the god Apollo and provides geographical and mythological histories for the locations mentioned in the poem.</meta>

**Just as from the temple** <note>original: *Oios d' ek neioio*</note>: the comparison is appropriate because Jason is young and Apollo is also young. **Throughout holy Delos** <note>original: *Delon an' egatheen*</note>: Delos is one of the Cyclades islands, sacred to Apollo. It was formerly called Delos <note>meaning "Manifest" or "Visible"</note>, but later called Asteria <note>meaning "Starry"</note> because of its shape. It was also called Ortygia <note>meaning "Quail Island"</note> after the sister of Leto <note>Apollo’s mother</note>. **Or Claros** <note>original: *He Klaron*</note>: Claros is a city near Colophon, sacred to Apollo. It contains an oracle of the god established there by Manto, the daughter of Tiresias <note>the famous blind seer of Thebes</note>; or perhaps it was named after a certain hero named Claros, as the author Thyorges suggests. But Nearchus says that:

<margin>
Apollo received the city by lot <note>original: *kleron*</note>; and from this "lot" it was thus named. Others say, following the painter Baïs, that Manto, daughter of Tiresias, was dedicated there as a "first-fruit offering" <note>original: *akrothinian*</note> by his descendants.
</margin>

> JUST AS APOLLO GOES FORTH FROM HIS FRAGRANT TEMPLE,
> THROUGH HOLY DELOS, OR CLAROS, OR PERHAPS PYTHO,
> OR BROAD LYCIA BY THE STREAMS OF THE XANTHUS;
> SUCH WAS HE AS HE PASSED THROUGH THE THRONG OF PEOPLE. AND A SHOUT AROSE
> AS THEY CHEERED TOGETHER. AND THERE AN ELDERLY WOMAN MET HIM,
> IPHIAS, THE PRIESTESS OF ARTEMIS, GUARDIAN OF THE CITY.
> AND SHE KISSED HIS RIGHT HAND. BUT SHE COULD NOT SAY A WORD
> NEVERTHELESS, THOUGH SHE LONGED TO, AS THE CROWD RUSHED FORWARD.
> BUT SHE WAS LEFT THERE AT THE SIDE, JUST AS THE ELDERLY
> ARE LEFT BY THE YOUNG. BUT HE, HAVING DIVERTED FROM THE MANY, STEPPED ASIDE.

The daughter <note>Manto</note> was sent to Delphi, and following an oracle of Apollo, she went out and encountered Rhacius, son of Lebes, a Mycenaean by birth. She was joined to him in his prime, for the oracle had declared she should marry whoever she first encountered. They went together to Colophon; and there, grieving, she wept for the destruction of her fatherland <note>Thebes</note>. Therefore, the place was named Claros from her "weeping" <note>original: *klarein*, an archaic word for crying</note>. For the letter 'L' is related to 'R' <note>a linguistic observation on liquid consonants</note>, just as the word for "watery" is sometimes spelled with an 'L' <note>original: *hydrelos*</note> instead of an 'R' <note>original: *hydreros*</note>. It is also said that a spring gushed up from Manto’s tears, and this is Claros. Or, that she herself established the oracle of Apollo there. Others say it was called Claros because Hesiloas and Archas "cast lots" <note>original: *klerosasthai*</note> there. As for Rhacius, he was named so because of his poverty or ill fortune. **Crowding** <note>original: *Kyklomenon*</note>: many people together calling out or cheering. **Met him** <note>original: *To d' exymbleto*</note>: it was a good omen <note>original: *symbolon*</note> that she was both elderly and a priestess, namely Iphias. **Nor could she say anything** <note>original: *Oude ti phathai*</note>: the letter 'eta' should be drawn out; nevertheless, though she was eager to speak, she did not manage it in time. The word *empes* <note>original: *empēs*</note> is used here to mean "nevertheless."

**They received** <note>original: *diedechato*</note>: This means they welcomed him, or they were waiting for him.

**Coming down** <note>original: *katablōskontas*</note>: This means descending or arriving. The letter "beta" (.b.) is used instead of "mu" (.m.) <note>an ancient linguistic observation; the commentator notes that the sounds of B and M are related</note>. From this also comes the word **altar** <note>original: *bōmos*</note>, derived from the word for "going" or "stepping" <note>original: *blōskein*</note> because one goes up to it.

Similarly, we see the phrase **lofty grain** <note>original: *siton blōthron*</note>, referring to grain that is tall and "reaches toward the upper air."

**Wrapped in a hide** <note>original: *derma d’ omen*</note>: This describes being covered or wrapped in a skin. This refers to the act of wearing a leather garment.

<meta>This page follows Jason’s arrival at the harbor of Pagasae, where he has just asked the crew to elect a leader for the quest. While the crew initially looked to Heracles, this page records the transition of leadership to Jason and the start of the physical preparations for the voyage.</meta>

"Let no one offer this glory to me," [Heracles said]. "For I will not yield; I will even stop anyone else from standing up. Let the man himself who gathered us together lead our company."

So he spoke with high resolve; and he gestured toward the young man <gloss>short vowel mark</gloss> <note>original: *hēitheon*; referring to Jason</note> as Heracles commanded. And Jason himself, a man of war, rose up glad at heart, and spoke to those who were eager for the journey:

"If you indeed entrust this glory to be my care, let our path no longer be checked as it was before. For now, let us appease Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of prophecy</note> with sacrifices and prepare a feast nearby. While my servants, the overseers of my stalls whose task it is, come here to drive oxen from the herd, let us meanwhile drag the ship into the sea. Once we have placed all the gear inside, we shall cast lots for the benches of the oars <note>original: *klēidos eretma*; technical term for the thole-pins where the oars are secured</note>. In the meantime, let us also build an altar on the shore to Apollo of the Embarkation <note>original: *Embasiou*; a specific title for Apollo as protector of those boarding ships</note>, who promised to signify and show to me the paths of the sea, if I begin my labors for the King by offering sacrifices to him."

He spoke, and was the first to turn to the work. They rose up in obedience to him; and they piled their garments in a heap upon a smooth, flat ledge of rock which the sea did not reach with its waves, for the wintry spray had washed it clean long ago. 

First of all, they girded the ship <gloss>long vowel mark</gloss> strongly under the guidance of Argus <note>the master-builder of the ship</note>, binding her from within with a well-twisted rope <note>This refers to 'frapping,' a nautical technique where cables are wrapped around the hull to prevent the timber planks from springing apart during a storm</note>. They pulled it tight on both sides so that the planks might be held fast by the bolts and withstand the opposing force of the surging sea. Then they quickly dug a trench as wide as the space the ship occupied, and as far as the bow reached out toward the sea...

Lustral water: <note>original: "cherniba"</note> <gloss>that with which they wash their hands</gloss>. Barley groats: <note>original: "oulochytas"</note> some say these are the baskets, because the sacrificial items are carried in them; others say it refers to the actual barley, since they threw whole barley grains onto the altars. City of Aeson: <note>original: "Aesonida"</note> a city in Magnesia named after Jason's father, as mentioned by Pindar and Pherecydes. Hellas. Some say that Hellas is synonymous with Phthia; however, we take Hellas to be a high country; <note>The commentator is distinguishing between a specific city or district and the broader region of Northern Greece.</note> certainly not the same as Phthia; and in this context, it refers to the whole of Hellas. Ortygia: Concerning Ortygia, Phanodicus has recorded history in his *Delian Affairs*; and Nicander in the third book of the *Aetolians* says that Delos was named after the Ortygia in Aetolia. <note>Ortygia, meaning "Quail Island," was a name associated with several locations, most famously Delos or an island near Syracuse.</note>

It is written <note>original: "Graph(etai)"</note> "om." Others say: "setting out from Ortygia of Tynis." Some said it was [Ephesus]; others, the one previously called Delos; others the island bordering Sicily; whence all Ortygias are celebrated, and Delos too... they are not mythologized as being named from the transformation of Asteria, the sister of Leto <note>According to myth, Asteria turned into a quail—*ortyx*—to escape Zeus, becoming the island Ortygia/Delos.</note>; but insofar as all Ortygias are colonies of the Ortygia in Aetolia.

Boarding-steps: <gloss>offerings for embarkation</gloss> for the sake of... metaphorically, for the sake of boarding the ship now for the first time. We have set before: <gloss>instead of "we perform"</gloss> or indeed "to cause to happen." Sacrificial meal: <gloss>barley-meal</gloss>. Some say the barley-grains; others the water which they are accustomed to pour into the ear of the sacrificial victim so that the animal might nod <note>In Greek ritual, the animal's "nod" (caused by the cold water) was interpreted as its willing consent to be sacrificed.</note>; others say the barley-meal. To gird oneself <note>original: "zosasthai"</note>: instead of setting to work or being prepared; it also signifies arming oneself.
<margin>au</margin> With a bronze axe. Apollonius says in the first book of his commentaries that iron was called "bronze" by the ancients. He is unaware that, since iron had not yet been discovered, they actually used bronze. As Hesiod also says: "They worked with bronze; for black iron did not yet exist." <note>The commentator is noting the "Bronze Age" setting of the poem, citing Hesiod's *Works and Days*.</note>

The phrasing **"bringing the fleece"**: it should have been "about to bring" or "having to bring" in relation to "for you." And the Poet also says: "It is always dear to you to be away from me." <note>Homer, *Iliad* 1.541. The commentator is discussing a grammatical point where a participle is used instead of an infinitive.</note> **Asia**: Asia was named after Asia, the mother of Prometheus and Atlas; others say it is from "thriving," having silt <note>original: "asin"—the commentator is exploring a folk etymology for Asia, linking it to the Greek word for river-silt or mud.</note>. **Thus having learned from evils**: not in general, but in my own harmful circumstances. This is a **hyperbaton** <term>Hyperbaton: A figure of speech where the natural word order is disrupted for emphasis, often by placing words far apart that belong together.</term> and the "and" conjunction is redundant. The preposition "from" is missing...

--- Page 39 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Argonauts’ preparations at Pagasae. After the sacrifice performed by Idmon and the omens seen in the smoke, the narrative shifts to the crew's final meal on land and the growing anxiety of their leader, Jason, before Idmon's prophecy is fully realized.</meta>

The writer uses the **Genitive case instead of the Dative**. <note>original: "Genike anti dotikes"</note> Also, the verb is in the **perfective** sense instead of "they went out." The meaning is as follows: "Having known my own fate beforehand from bad omens, I went out from the palace so that by advising you I might bring back glory." **So that I might embark**: this is a transposition; the sequence should be "so that I might embark upon the ship." For one embarking on the ship, the house of Doxias <note>A reference to Apollo, the god of prophecy, often called Loxias; "Doxia" here may be a scribal variant or specific local title.</note> would be left behind. **Stationary**: used instead of "scorching" and "hot."

**NOW WHEN THE SUN IN THE STATIONARY PART OF THE DAY PASSES BY,**
**AND THE FIELDS ARE NEWLY SHADOWED BY THE CLIFFS**
**AS THE SUN TILTS TOWARD THE DUSK OF THE WEST,**
**THEN THEY ALL POURED OUT A DEEP BED OF LEAVES**
**UPON THE SANDS IN FRONT OF THE GREY SHORE.**
**THEY RECLINED IN ORDER. AND BESIDE THEM LAY COUNTLESS**
**FOODS AND SWEET WINE, DRAWN IN PITCHERS BY THE**
**CUPBEARERS. AND AFTERWARD, THEY SPOKE TO ONE ANOTHER**
**IN TURNS, JUST AS YOUNG MEN OFTEN DO AT FEASTS AND OVER WINE,**
**CHEERFULLY BANTERING, WHEN INSATIABLE INSOLENCE IS ABSENT.**
**THERE AGAIN THE SON OF AESON, HELPLESS WITHIN HIMSELF,**
**WAS BROODING OVER EACH DETAIL, LOOKING LIKE ONE DOWNCAST.**
**AND IDAS, PERCEIVING HIM, REBUKED HIM WITH A LOUD VOICE:**
**"SON OF AESON, WHAT PLAN IS THIS YOU REVOLVE IN YOUR MIND?**
**SPEAK YOUR THOUGHT IN THE MIDST. OR DOES FEAR OVERCOME YOU,**
**WHICH TERRIFIES COWARDLY MEN?"**

<column-break/>

The author describes **noon** <note>original: "mesembria"</note> from its effects; since the sun, having reached the middle of heaven, heats all things. This is because it is equally distant from every direction for those watching. Or, it is called "stationary" because the sun then does not seem to move at all. **Of the grey [sea]**: because it is washed away by the waves, being dashed by them.

<column-break/>

By **bed of leaves**, he means a pallet made of foliage. **Sweet** (*laron*): derived from "very fitting" <note>original: "lian areros"</note>. Or it is formed from the word for "to wish" (*lo*). Hesiod says "sweet" and "pleasing to the sight." **Bantering** (*ephiōntai*): from the word for "play," which is a game played through words. It is like a "word-play" (*epesia*), coming from *epos* (word). For this reason, it has a "smooth breathing" <note>An Ancient Greek grammatical mark indicating the lack of an initial "h" sound.</note>. When it has a "rough breathing" (sounding like "hepsiontai"), it means "they follow." **Insatiable** (*aatos*): that which is very harmful; for the first "a" is an intensifier, as in "gaping" or "untiring." **Brooding** (*porphyresken*): instead of "he pondered in the depths." For the "purple-fish" (*porphyra*) is a kind of sea-creature found in the depths of the sea. Jason was therefore anxious about the dangers of both the land and the sea.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the conflict between Idas and the seer Idmon during the Argonauts' departure feast. He laughed out loud; and this is a sign of frivolity <note>original: "kouphotetos." Literally "lightness" of character or lack of seriousness.</note>, as Isocrates says: *do not be fond of headlong laughter.* <note>A reference to Isocrates’ *To Demonicus* 15, advising a young man on proper conduct.</note> **With mocking words** <note>original: "Kertomioisin."</note>: this refers to speech that is "speechless" <note>likely meaning "not to be spoken" or "unspeakable"</note> or able to "cut the heart" <note>original: "to kear temnein." A popular ancient etymology for *kertomein* (to mock).</note> and cause pain. **Squinting**: mocking him with his eyes; for those who are cross-eyed are called "squint-eyed" <note>original: "epilloi."</note>. **Come now**: here he mocks Idmon in two ways: first, as a simple seer who lacks real skill <note>original: "atechnos mantis."</note>, and second, as one who takes too much pride in his father Apollo.

<margin>
...as one who is greatly able to bring down the arrogant. He does this with deceptive speech. **Need** <note>original: "Chreio."</note> denotes both that which proceeds with necessity and fate, and that which is to come. **With regret** <note>original: "metamolion."</note> means "worthy of regret." It is also written as "fruitless" <note>original: "metamonion."</note>, which means vain or useless.
</margin>

->WERE ONCE JOINED TOGETHER IN A SINGLE FORM.<-

**Borne with the winds**: the word "fruitless" <note>original: "metamonion."</note> comes from the plural genitive of "winds" <note>original: "anemon."</note> and becomes a possessive adjective; it has an *iota* in the second to last syllable, like "fortunate" <note>original: "tycheios."</note>. For example: *of winds* [anemon] becomes *windy* [anemonios]. **Raging and rebuking**: he was angry and enraged, speaking ill of him and blaming him. **In his left hand** <note>original: "laie."</note>: used by way of euphemism <note>Ancient Greeks sometimes avoided the direct word for "left" (aristera) because of its unlucky associations, using "laie" or "euonymos" instead.</note> for the left hand. **Began** <note>original: "peirazen."</note>: used here instead of "tuned" or "fitted" the song. The word "up" <note>original: "ana," in "anaschomenos."</note> is redundant. The sense of the passage is: *and Orpheus, <unclear>instead</unclear> of standing up, spoke.* See here the usefulness of music, if indeed it puts a stop to outbursts and contentions. **He sang how the earth**: the poet wants to show the first "confusion" <note>original: "synchysis." Referring to the primordial Chaos.</note> of the elements as a sort of contention, from which each thing took its own portion and order. The song is appropriate to the present circumstances, showing that it is fitting to cease from battle and return to one's proper disposition.

Anaxagoras, calling it a kind of molten mass <note>original: "mydron." A red-hot stone or metal mass.</note>, says it is that from which the stars are made. Wherefore, in the *Fans* <note>original: "Ripitioi." Likely a lost satirical work or play.</note>, someone known to him mockingly said the sun was a "golden clod." Regarding the moon, the same Anaxagoras...
</margin>

**From deadly Strife**: Empedocles says that when all things were previously mixed together, Strife <note>original: "Neikos." The force of separation.</note> and Love <note>original: "Philia." The force of attraction.</note> were sent forth and brought about separation; without these, he claims nothing can come into being. It follows, as is likely, that nothing is ever truly destroyed. Meanwhile, Thales established water as the first principle of all things, taking this from "the Poet" <note>Homer</note> who says: *But may you all become water and earth.* Likewise, some say that Hesiod’s "Chaos" is actually water, from which mud is settled. As this mud hardens, the earth is solidified.

Thirdly, he says that Love <note>Eros</note> came into being...

[Chaos] reveals a wide space <note>An ancient etymological play on *Chaos* meaning "yawning gap."</note>. In this space, the Nemean lion is said to have fallen <note>Referring to the myth that the lion fell from the moon.</note>. **Dictaean**: the Cretan mountain where Zeus was raised, as Callimachus records. **Not yet [armed him]**: Duris <note>Duris of Samos, a Greek historian.</note> says that the stones thrown down by the Giants <note>during their battle with the gods</note> became islands if they fell into the sea, and mountains if they fell on land.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Argonauts’ reaction to the song of Orpheus. **They, insatiably** <note>original: "Toi d' amoton."</note>: meaning "unceasingly" and "without being filled." Nor did their minds rest when the song ceased, but being still unsatisfied by it, they leaned their heads forward, straining their ears <note>original: "amatelakoton" — likely a scribal error for "anatetakoton," meaning straining or cocking the ears.</note> and resting in silence. They were held fast by such pleasure.

<margin>**By the enchantment.** <note>original: "Kelethmo."</note></margin>

In the pre-edition <note>An earlier version of the *Argonautica* that differed from the one that survived to the Middle Ages.</note> after this, it was written: "When the dawn appeared... and then to the night (they sacrificed to the Far-Darter <note>Apollo</note> right there for those who were being struck), then a wind from Zeus fell upon them. Tiphys was roused, urging them to go to the benches. They heard..." and then follows the text currently laid out: "and the harbor was terrible; nor for long afterward." Thus one must

**THEY, INSATIABLY, EVEN THOUGH HE HAD CEASED, STILL LEANED THEIR HEADS FORWARD.**
**ALL ALIKE WITH EARS UPRIGHT, RESTING IN SILENCE,**
**BY THE ENCHANTMENT OF SUCH A CHARMING SONG THAT LINGERED WITHIN THEM.**
**NOR FOR LONG AFTERWARD DID THEY MIX THE LIBATIONS,**
**AS IS CUSTOM, WHICH THEY THEN POURED UPON THE TONGUES.**

**As is custom** <note>original: "He themis."</note>: Because it was the habit of the ancients to mix a bowl of wine when they were about to sleep and to sacrifice the tongues of the sacrificial animals to Hermes and pour wine over them. Perhaps there is a natural reason for this: since Hermes is traditionally handed down as being "Reason" <note>original: "Logos."</note>, and the tongue is his instrument, it rests when sleep falls upon a person. Therefore, they appropriately sacrifice it to Hermes. Even Homer says: *They cast the tongues into the fire.* 

Diarchidas, in his *History of Megara*, relates that Alcathous, the son of Pelops, was exiled from Megara because of the murder of Chrysippus and set out to settle in another city. Encountering a lion that was ravaging Megara—though others say people were sent by the King of the Megarians to fight it—he cut out its tongue, placed it in his pouch, and returned again to Megara. When he met <gloss>after a <unclear>time</unclear></gloss> those who had been sent on the hunt claiming that they were the ones who had conquered it, he brought forth the beast, produced the pouch, and refuted them. Because of this, the King, when arranging the sacrifice, placed the tongue on the altars last of all. From that time on, this custom remained among the Megarians.

Philochorus, in his work *On Sacrifices*, says that the tongue is the finest and most excellent part of the body. And Homer says: *But come, cut the tongues,* meaning "cease your speeches."

<meta>This page transitions from the crew’s silent enchantment following Orpheus’ song to the physical preparations for their departure. It provides both the poetic narrative of the Argo’s launch and a scholarly commentary on the ship's divine construction and the massive physical presence of the hero Heracles.</meta>

**...for in it was the timber.** <note>original: "en gar hoi dory"</note> He says, quite convincingly, that the wood in the *Argo* is from the **Dodonian oak** and was "endowed with voice" <note>original: "phonēen"</note>; since even the tree itself used to speak, as **Homer** says: "so that from the high-leafed oak he might hear the counsel of the god." <note>A reference to the Oracle of Dodona, where priests interpreted the rustling of oak leaves as the voice of Zeus.</note> **And they [went] to the benches** <note>original: "hoi d' amai selmata"</note>: the rowing seats or the deck-planks. Generally, any broad plank is called a *selma* or *selidoma*; which is also why we call the <term>columns: "selidas," the vertical sections of text on a scroll</term> of the **rhapsodies** <note>performances of epic poetry</note> by this name, because of their breadth.

**Was washed under.** <note>original: "Hypai hypeklysthē"</note> This refers to the ship being weighed down as he sat...

<column-break/>

...with prayers. They were reminded of sleep by the darkness.
**But when gleaming Dawn with her bright eyes**
**beheld the steep peaks of Pelion, and the calm**
**headlands were washed by the wind-tossed sea,**
**it was then that Tiphys awoke; and at once he roused his companions**
**to board the ship and make ready the oars.**
**Terrible was the sound from the harbor of Pagasae; and even the**
**Pelian Argo herself cried out, urging them to depart.**
**For in her was fixed a divine beam, which Athena**
**had fitted into the middle of the keel, made of Dodonian oak.**
**And they went up to the benches one after another**
**as they had previously divided the rowing spots among themselves,**
**sitting in good order by their own gear.**
**In the middle sat Ancaeus and the great strength of Heracles;**
**beside him he placed his club, and beneath his feet**
**the keel of the ship was submerged.** <note>A poetic detail emphasizing Heracles' semi-divine, massive weight compared to ordinary men.</note> **The cables were already being hauled in**
**and they poured wine over the sea; but Jason,**
**tearful, turned his eyes away from his fatherland.**
**And they, like youths [dancing] for Phoebus [Apollo] at Pytho or Delos...**

---

->**COMMENTARY**<-

He says it was "washed over" <note>original: "epiklysthē"</note> rather than simply "washed under," meaning the sinking of the ship occurred deep into the sea due to the sheer weight of the hero <note>Heracles</note>. **Either in Pytho or in Delos**: The sense of the passage is as follows: just as he says that in **Delphi** <note>Pytho</note> or **Delos** or by the **Ismenus** <note>a river in Thebes</note> people set up a dance around the altar of **Apollo** and strike the ground with their feet in harmony with the melody of the lyre; so these men too, enchanted by the lyre of **Orpheus**, moved more vigorously to their rowing. The following phrase "all together" <note>original: "homartē"</note> indicates a lengthening of the sound. The preposition "under" <note>original: "hypo"</note> is redundant here, as in the phrase: "he dragged the bottom of the plow-share under." <note>A technical grammatical note comparing the poet's use of prepositions to archaic Homeric style.</note>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the *Argo’s* departure from the coast of Thessaly. While the previous page described the gods watching the ship, this section focuses on the specific local myths of the region they are passing, particularly the appearance of the Centaur Chiron and the education of the heroes Jason and Achilles.</meta>

...or rather from the Thessalian Itonia. <note>A reference to the title of Athena mentioned on the previous page.</note> Regarding her, Hecataeus says in the first book of his *Histories*—and Armenidas in his *Thebaica* says—that Itonus, the son of Amphictyon, was born in Thessaly. From him comes the city of Iton and Itonian Athena. Alexander also mentions this in the first book of his *Carian Commentaries*. **On the gray breaking of the wave.** <note>original: "poliē d' epi kymatos agē"</note> This refers to the shore where the waves are broken. Suidas, in his *Thessalian History*, says that Chiron is the son of Ixion. However:

<margin>
Setting aside the rest of the Centaurs <note>who were often depicted as wild and violent</note>, the author of the *Gigantomachy* <note>The War of the Giants</note> says that Cronus, having transformed himself into a horse, mingled with Philyra, the daughter of Oceanus; for this reason, Chiron was born as a horse-centaur.
</margin>

> BUT HE CAME DOWN FROM THE HIGH MOUNTAIN NEAR THE SEA,
> CHIRON THE SON OF PHILYRA; AND UPON THE GRAY BREAKING OF THE WAVE
> HE WET HIS FEET; AND OFTEN WAVING WITH HIS HEAVY HAND,
> HE SHOUTED GOOD LUCK FOR THE JOURNEY TO THOSE RETURNING WITHOUT SORROW;
> WITH HIM HIS WIFE, CARRYING IN HER ARMS
> THE SON OF PELEUS, ACHILLES, WAS SHOWING HIM TO HIS DEAR FATHER.
> AND WHEN THEY LEFT THE CURVING SHORE OF THE HARBOR,
> BY THE COUNSEL AND MIND OF THE PRUDENT SON OF AGNIAS,
> TIPHYS, WHO WITH HIS HANDS SKILLFULLY GUIDED
> THE WELL-POLISHED RUDDER TO KEEP IT STEADFAST AND DIRECTED OUTWARD.

His wife was Chariclo. It was fitting for the poet to introduce the image of Chiron here, both because he is a friend to mankind and the most just of the Centaurs, and because of his close relationship with his friends, particularly Jason. For it was from him that Jason learned the art of medicine; which is why he was named Jason, from the word for "healing." <note>original: "iasin" — the poet suggests the name Iasōn (Jason) is derived from iasis (healing/curing).</note> **Achilles, son of Peleus.** <note>original: "Pēleidēn Achilēa"</note> Apollonius followed the poets who came after Homer in saying that Achilles was raised by Chiron. Homer says no such thing; authors have also disagreed regarding his mother. Homer everywhere declares him to be the son of the sea-nymph Thetis. Lysimachus of Alexandria, speaking word-for-word in the second book of the *Returns* <note>original: "Nostoi," a lost cycle of epic poems about heroes returning from Troy</note>, notes this. For Suidas and Aristotle, when recording the history of Euboea, and the author of the *Phrygian Tales*, as well as Deimachus and Dionysius of Chalcis, did not let the common rumor about Achilles simply stand; on the contrary, some of them believe he was born of a different Thetis, the daughter of Chiron. Deimachus, however, says he was born of Philomela, the daughter of Actor. Other men declare different things about him.

<meta>This page continues the technical and mythological commentary on the voyage of the *Argo*. Having described the departure from the harbor and the farewell from Chiron on the previous page, the text now focuses on the specific nautical terminology used to describe the ship's rigging and the beginning of the journey past the Thessalian coast.</meta>

**The Mast-Step:** <note>original: "Mesodmē"</note> This is the socket or cross-beam where the mast is placed and tilted. **Forestays** <note>original: "Protonous"</note> are the ropes extending from either side of the mast toward the prow and the stern. The **top-mast** <note>original: "ēlakatē," literally 'distaff'</note> refers to the thinnest and highest part of the mast; according to Eratosthenes, the **mast-head** <note>original: "karchēsion," a cup-shaped structure for lookouts or pulleys</note> sits above this. Regarding the **deck-planking** <note>original: "ikrion"</note>, some call it a part of the mast itself, but it is better to understand it as the **yardarm** <note>original: "keraia"</note> and its outer ends. The term "deck-planking" also refers to the wooden boards to which the pins are attached. **Pins** <note>original: "pyronas" or "peronēs"</note> refers to 

<margin>
the pegs upon
the planking,
also called 
**bolts** <note>original: "gomphous"</note>,
to which they 
bind the ropes.
**Cables** <note>original: "kalōs"</note>
are the ropes 
which, in this 
context, hold 
the mast steady 
from each side 
of the ship.
</margin>

> THEN INDEED THEY RAISED THE GREAT MAST IN THE MAST-STEP.
> THEY BOUND IT WITH FORESTAYS, STRETCHING THEM TIGHT ON EITHER SIDE.
> THEY LET DOWN THE LINEN SAILS, PULLING THEM UP TO THE TOP-MAST.
> A WHISTLING WIND FELL UPON THE SAILS; AND THE CABLES
> THEY FASTENED TO POLISHED PINS, DISTRIBUTING THEM ROUND ABOUT.
> THEY PASSED THE TISAEAN PROMONTORY, BEYOND THE LONG DIVINE HEADLAND.
> For them, the son of Oeagrus <note>Orpheus</note> played the lyre with a well-ordered song,
> singing from the ship of the noble daughter of a noble father,
> ARTEMIS. SHE WHO WATCHED OVER THOSE SEA-CLIFFS,
> PROTECTING THE LAND OF IOLCUS. AND TO THEM, FROM THE DEEP,
> fishes came darting over the sea-foam, mingling with the proud waves.

---

In general, every rope is called a **cable** <note>original: "kalōs"</note>. Because of this, scholars distinguish between them: the ropes used to lower the sail are called **mid-stays** <note>original: "mesourias"</note>. Those used to strengthen the mast from each side toward the prow are called **forestays**. The ropes at the corners of the sails are **sheets** <note>original: "podas," literally 'feet'</note>, and those following after them are the **fore-runners** <note>original: "prodromos"</note>. In the middle are the ropes called **yard-arm stays** <note>original: "terthrioi"</note>, followed by those simply called the "middle ropes." The term **distinguishingly** <note>original: "diakridon"</note> means "distinctly" and "in an extended manner." Therefore, when the poet says "they pulled the linens to the top-mast," he means they hauled the sails up to the very highest point of the mast. 

It should be noted that **Eratosthenes** <note>An Alexandrian scholar and polymath</note> in his work *On Architecture* says the parts of the mast are as follows:
*   **The Heel** <note>original: "pternēn," the bottom of the mast</note>
*   **The Chest** <note>original: "thōrakion," the mid-section</note>
*   **The Top-mast** <note>original: "ēlakatē"</note>
*   **The Mast-head** <note>original: "karchēsion"</note>
*   **The Yardarm** <note>original: "keraia"</note>
*   **The Deck-platform** <note>original: "ikrion"</note>

**Tisaeon** is a mountain peak in Thessaly; though some say it is in Magnesia. **Well-ordered** <note>original: "euthēmoni"</note> means well-arranged, in rhythm, or skillfully composed.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on the "Argonautica" by Apollonius Rhodius. Having described the ship's departure and the initial setting of the sails, the text now transitions into a famous simile comparing the fish following Orpheus’s music to sheep following a shepherd. "To show" <note>original: "phainai"</note> is used here for "to make." He hymns Artemis because the place mentioned is sacred to her.

**Immense** <note>original: "Apletoi"</note>: These are unapproachable or exceptionally large creatures. The term **skipping and swimming through** <note>original: "diaskairontes kai dianechomenoi"</note> refers to the fish; due to the lack of a strict meter here, it signifies the enchanting power of the melody. It is as if they are no longer harming one another but are following in peace. 

**Shepherd’s song** <note>original: "Nomion melos"</note>: A pastoral tune named after **shepherds** <note>original: "nomeas"</note>; or, this was simply what the ancients called a specific type of hymn. 

**Misty** <note>original: "Eēriē"</note>: This refers to either Crete or Thessaly, because the earth there is dark; indeed, they say Egypt is also called "misty" for this reason. Alternatively, "misty" <note>original: "ēeria"</note> might mean "early," derived from the word for **dawn** <note>original: "ēri"</note>. 

**Pelasgians**: This refers to the Thessalians, descended from Pelasgus, the son of

...claims that Pelasgus was Argive by race but migrated to Thessaly, and that Thessaly was named Pelasgia after him. Sophocles, in his play *Inachus*, says that the Argives themselves were called Pelasgians, and that the Tyrrhenians were also Pelasgians. 

**Cliffs** <note>original: "Eripnas"</note>: These are broken-off hills, crags, or caves in the cliffs. Some use this term for houses because they are "firmly fixed" <note>original: "erēreistai"</note>. The word **cliff** <note>original: "eripnē"</note> is used for a headland because it is **excessively blown** <note>original: "agan pneesthai"</note> by the wind. 

**Sepias**: A headland in the region of Iolcus. It is named thus because **Thetis** <note>the sea-goddess and mother of Achilles</note> was transformed there into a **cuttlefish** <note>original: "sepia"</note> while she was being pursued by Peleus. 

**Skiathos by the sea**: This refers to the island's location along the coastline.

For the island of **Skiathos** <note>original: "Skiathos"</note> is near Thessaly and Euboea, which Simonides also mentions. **Peiresiai** <note>original: "Peiresiai"</note> is a city in Magnesia. **Magnesa** <note>original: "Magnesa"</note> is a city eponymous with the region; it is exceptionally **calm** <note>original: "eudios"</note> and located by the sea. He stayed by the shore, as Cleon says in the first book of the *Argonautica*. To those who have passed away, they offer sacrifices <note>The term for sacrifice to the dead is "enagizein," whereas "thyein" is for the gods.</note> at the setting of the sun; but to the heavenly gods, they sacrifice toward the dawn as the sun rises. **Slaughtered-sacrifices** <note>original: "entoma"</note> specifically refers to the victims offered to the dead because their heads are cut off <note>The root "temno" means to cut; "entoma" suggests cutting into a pit in the earth.</note> over the ground. For this is how they sacrifice to the **underworld gods** <note>original: "chthoniois"</note>; but for the heavenly gods, they pull back the neck to face upward and then slaughter. <note>Abbreviated as Homer</note> Homer says: "First they drew back the heads [of the victims]..." Others say **slaughtered-sacrifices** <note>original: "entoma"</note> refers to the dead as being "unproductive" victims for the "unproductive" departed, whereas for the heavenly gods, they sacrificed potent, uncastrated animals. The preposition "near" <note>original: "para"</note> is omitted here, so it should read that they sacrificed to Dolops "near" the swell of the sea.

**They tarried** <note>original: "Elinyēskon"</note>: They stayed in the same place or rested because they were hindered on their journey.

**Meliboea** <note>original: "Meliboia"</note>: A city of Thessaly.

**Homole** <note>original: "Homole"</note>: Homole is a mountain in Thessaly so called, or perhaps a city in Thrace. **Nor for long** <note>original: "oude ti deron"</note>: the meaning is that after this point, the currents of the river do not pass for long. The city was named after Myrina, the wife of Thoas and daughter of Cretheus. **And even as far as** <note>original: "kai esachri"</note>: here the word "and" is superfluous to the meaning.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on the Argonautica of Apollonius Rhodius. Following the voyage past Mount Athos, the Argonauts now arrive at the island of Lemnos, setting the stage for one of the most famous and dark episodes of the journey—the story of the Lemnian women who murdered their husbands.</meta>

**Sintian** <note>original: "Sinteida"</note>: Used as an epithet for the island of **Lemnos** <note>An island in the northern Aegean Sea</note>. The **Tyrrhenians** <note>A non-Greek people often identified with the Etruscans or early pirates</note> were the first to inhabit it, being most harmful people; and because of this, it was inhabited by "barbarians." Even **Homer** <note>The legendary author of the Iliad and Odyssey</note> says: "He went to Lemnos among the Sintian men of wild speech." But **Hellanicus** <note>A 5th-century BCE Greek historian</note> says that the Lemnians were named **Sintians** <note>original: "Sintias"</note> because they were the first to create weapons of war for the purpose of **harming** <note>original: "sinesthai," a pun on the name Sintian</note> and injuring their neighbors. **At once** <note>original: "Amudis"</note>: the Lemnian women, having for a long time neglected the honors due to **Aphrodite** <note>The goddess of love and beauty</note>, stirred the goddess to anger against them.

<margin>
For she cast a **foul odor** <note>original: "lysos," though usually "dysosmia"</note> upon them all, so that they no longer pleased their husbands. The men, having gone to war against the **Thracians**, took many female captives from there, and turned away from their lawful wives.
</margin>

## **FOR THEM THAT SAME DAY AND UNTIL DUSK THE WIND WAS**
## **ENTIRELY FRESH; AND THE SAILS OF THE SHIP WERE STRAINED.**
## **BUT TOGETHER WITH THE RAYS OF THE SUN, AS THE WIND FAILED,**
## **BY ROWING THEY REACHED ROCKY SINTIAN LEMNOS.**
## **THERE, AT ONCE, THE WHOLE PEOPLE, BY THE TRANSGRESSION OF THE WOMEN,**
## **HAD BEEN RUTHLESSLY SLAIN IN THE YEAR JUST PASSED.**
## **FOR INDEED, THE MEN HAD REJECTED THEIR WEDDED WIVES,**
## **HAVING COME TO HATE THEM, AND HELD FOR CAPTIVE WOMEN**
## **A HARSH PASSION. THESE THEY THEMSELVES HAD BROUGHT FROM THE OPPOSITE SHORE**
## **WHILE RAVAGING THRACE; BECAUSE A TERRIBLE WRATH HAD BEEN SENT**
## **BY CYPRIS. FOR THEY HAD LONG NEGLECTED HER HONORS.**
## **O WRETCHED WOMEN! INSATIABLE IN THEIR MOST MISERABLE JEALOUSY.**

Against the goddess, the women voted by oath to kill their husbands at night. And they did not only do this, but they also killed the captives. Fearing that the children, once they became men, would take revenge on them, they killed the entire male race at once. **From the opposite shore** <note>original: "Antiperethen"</note>: meaning from the side facing them, for that is how **Thrace** <note>The region north of the Aegean</note> is situated in relation to Lemnos. **Captives** <note>original: "leiadas"</note> refers to the women taken in war. **Neglected** <note>original: "aitisan"</note>: they did not honor. It should be known by those who study these things that due to the wrath of Aphrodite, the Lemnian women developed a foul smell. **Myrtilus** <note>An ancient historian from Lesbos</note> in the first book of his *Lesbian History* disagrees; he says that **Medea** <note>The famous sorceress who would later join the Argonauts</note>, while sailing past, threw a magical drug into Lemnos out of jealousy, and thus a foul odor arose among the women. He claims that even until now, there is a certain day each year when, because of this stench, the men and sons keep away from the women.

<summary>This page explains the backstory of the "Lemnian Crime," where the women of Lemnos murdered all the men on the island. It explores the dual reasons for this—either a curse of foul odor from the goddess Aphrodite or a magical poisoning by Medea.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Lemnian massacre. The previous page ended mid-sentence describing how the male population had been slaughtered by the women of Lemnos, with the exception of Hypsipyle’s father.</meta>

It was out of all the women that Hypsipyle rightly chose not to kill her father. First, because as a daughter, she provided the safety owed to Thoas <note>Hypsipyle was the daughter of King Thoas of Lemnos</note>. Second, because of his advanced age. Or, perhaps, because he himself was neither responsible for nor a collaborator in the **insolence** <note>original: "aselgeias," referring to the men's neglect of their wives</note> of the other Lemnians. They drew him to Oinoie; the historian Theolytus records this story. Sicinus is an island—

<margin>
—a certain island off the coast of Euboea; it was previously called Oinoie <note>original: "Oinoie," meaning "Wine-land"</note> because it was **planted with vines**. Both Cleon of Curium and Asclepiades of Myrlea record that Thoas was saved there; this shows that Apollonius <note>The author of the Argonautica</note> took all his material from Cleon.

**Not alone with their own husbands did they destroy them**
**in their beds, but the entire male race together; so that afterwards**
**they might not pay any retribution for the grim murder.**

**Thoas, who then ruled over the people.**
**She set him in a hollow chest to be carried over the sea,**
**if he might escape. And he was drawn to Oinoie**
**before, but it was called the island of Sicinus later,**
**after the fishermen from Sicinus, whom the Naiad**
**nymph Oinoie bore when she lay with Thoas.**
**For them, tending herds of cattle, donning bronze**
**armor, and plowing the wheat-bearing fields**
**was easier than the works of Athena** <note>The "works of Athena" refers to traditional feminine domestic tasks like weaving and spinning</note>,
**which they used to do before. Yet for all that,**
**they were often glancing over the wide sea with their eyes**
**in terrible dread, whenever the Thracians might come.**

Cleon of Curium records this and Asclepiades of Myrlea; this shows that Apollonius took everything from Cleon. **Fishermen** <term>original: "epakteres" — while this word can mean hunters, the commentator notes that on an island it must mean those who hunt the sea, i.e., fishermen</term>. **For them, tending herds**: for the rest of the time, because the island remained empty of men, necessity and experience changed the women to a **manly way of life** and occupation. **Yet often they looked**: the conjunction "or" <note>original: "ē"</note> here is equivalent to the word "indeed" <note>original: "dē"</note>. This is just as it is used in **Homer** <note>The famous epic poet</note>: "Indeed <note>original: "ē dē"</note> it is disastrous." It is used in a parallel sense.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the arrival of the Argonauts at Lemnos. The previous page discussed the Lemnian women's massacre of their husbands and Hypsipyle's secret rescue of her father, King Thoas, who was set adrift and eventually reached the island of Oinoie (later renamed Sicinus).</meta>

For they <note>the Lemnian women</note> said they were approaching as if for war. Myrine is a city of Lemnos, which was mentioned earlier. **Like raw-flesh-eating Thyads** <note>original: "Thyasin omoborois," referring to the raving followers of Dionysus who tore animals apart with their bare hands</note>. In that context, they also call Semele "Thyone," because Aeschylus represented her as being pregnant and in a state of divine frenzy <note>original: "enthyazomenen"</note>. Similarly, he described those who touched her womb as being in a different kind of frenzy. In other words, like Maenads or Bacchantes. The name "Thyone" for Semele comes from the word meaning "to rush" <note>original: "thyein"</note> or "to set in motion."

**AND WHEN THEY SAW THE ARGO BEING ROWED NEAR THE ISLAND,**
**IMMEDIATELY IN FULL FORCE OUTSIDE THE GATES OF MYRINE**
**THEY POURED FORTH TO THE SHORE IN HOSTILE ARMOR,**
**LIKE RAW-FLESH-EATING THYADS. FOR THEY THOUGHT**
**THE THRACIANS WERE COMING. OR WITH THEM, HYPSIPYLE,**
**DAUGHTER OF THOAS, PUT ON HER FATHER’S ARMOR;**
**THEY WERE POURED OUT SPEECHLESS IN HELPLESSNESS.**
**SUCH A FEAR HOVERED OVER THEM.**
**MEANWHILE, THE HEROES SENT FORTH FROM THE SHIP**
**AETHALIDES THE SWIFT HERALD. TO HIM THEY ENTRUSTED**
**THE MESSAGES AND THE SCEPTER OF HERMES,**
**HIS OWN FATHER, WHO GRANTED HIM A MEMORY OF ALL THINGS**
**UNFAILING; AND NOT EVEN NOW, THOUGH HE HAS DEPARTED FOR**
**THE UNSPOKEN EDDIES OF ACHERON, HAS FORGETFULNESS OVERTAKEN HIS SOUL.**

<column-break/>

The term refers to those who are maddened. Regarding **raw-flesh-eating** <note>original: "omoborois"</note>: this is because when they are seized by madness, they often eat raw, torn flesh, as Euripides says in his play, *The Bacchae*. **Daughter of Thoas** <note>original: "Thoantias"</note>: there are two forms for feminine patronymics <note>names derived from a father</note>. One ends in "-as," such as "Polias," and

---

the other ends in "-is," such as "Pelopis." In this case, it changes the final syllable to "-as" to avoid a harsh sound <note>original: "kakophona"</note>. **Meanwhile, from the ship**: this refers to the time during which the women were arming themselves. The word for "meanwhile" <note>original: "teios"</note> is an extended form used in place of "until" <note>original: "heos"</note>. **His own** <note>original: "sphoiterioio"</note>: the author here inappropriately used the dual form <note>a grammatical form referring to exactly two people</note> instead of the singular. **Unspoken** <note>original: "aprophatous"</note>: meaning things that cannot be addressed or explained. **Forgetfulness has overtaken**: it is said that the dead receive a forgetfulness <note>original: "Lethe"</note> of the events that happened during their life; but the author says that even though this man is dead, he did not fall into forgetfulness. This is either because of the doctrine of reincarnation held by the philosophers, or because of the specific will of the god Hermes.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the arrival of the Argonauts at Lemnos.
