He <note>Pherecydes</note> says that he first became Aethalides; then Euphorbus the hero; then a son of Hermes born from a certain courtesan; and finally Pythagoras. Memory followed him because Hermes granted this favor to Aethalides, to whom [it belongs]. "It is allotted" <note>original: "memoretai"</note> and the following terms are taken from [this tradition]...
</margin>

Pherecydes <note>an early Greek thinker from the 6th century BCE</note> says that Aethalides received a gift from the god Hermes: that his soul would sometimes be in the Underworld <note>original: "Hades"</note> and sometimes in the regions above the earth. The followers of Pythagoras <note>the Pythagoreans</note> say that since his soul was immortal, he was reborn during various life-cycles. First, he was Euphorbus, the son of Panthous <note>a Trojan hero mentioned in the Iliad</note>; after him, he became Pyrrhus the Cretan; then a certain man from Elis whose name is unknown; and after these incarnations, he became Pythagoras himself. Pythagoras believed in the migration of souls <note>metempsychosis</note> and their "clothing in flesh" <note>original: "sarkodynein," referring to the soul's entry into physical bodies</note> as they pass into other bodies.

"Things received from the gods"; for the word "it is allotted" <note>original: "memoira-tai"</note> means it has been assigned by lot. Aethalides, the herald of the Argonauts, was "alternating days" <note>original: "heteremeros"</note> as the author says; this means he spends one day in the Underworld and one day in the daylight. **Appeased** <note>original: "Meilixato"</note>: he exhorted or persuaded them with speech, being a man of great intellect. This phrasing follows the Homeric style: "It is a good thing when a messenger knows what is fitting." **Of the day coming to an end**: this refers to the "release" or finishing of the day. **Cables** <note>original: "Peismata"</note>: these are the ropes attached to the prow of the ship. The logic of the passage is this: even though the blowing of the North wind <note>original: "Boreas"</note> was favorable for the Argonauts' voyage, they nevertheless did not untie their ropes <note>because they were waiting for the herald's negotiation</note>.

<meta>This page continues the detailed description of the mythological scenes on Jason's purple cloak. Having just described the building of Thebes by the brothers Amphion and Zethus, the commentator now explores the symbolic contrast between their methods—brute strength versus the power of music—before moving to the next embroidered scene: Aphrodite holding the shield of Ares and the battle for the cattle of Electryon.</meta>

**Double**; <note>original: "Di-"</note> refers to "twice as large," as in the weight he carried. This signifies nothing other than the virtue of music and refined education <note>original: "eupaideusia"</note> compared to irrational, brute bravery. It suggests that while the one [Zethus], being very strong, could carry only a little despite his great toil, the other [Amphion] was able to carry the greatest weight through the power of his education. **Swift**; <note>original: "thoos"</note> means that which is moving and easily shifted, derived from the word "to hasten" <note>original: "thoazein"</note>. **Holding**; <note>original: "ochmazousa"</note> means restraining or carrying; even though she is not a warlike goddess, she does this as a favor to her lover Ares. Properly, the word "to hold" <note>original: "ochmasai"</note> means to lead a horse under a bridle or a chariot. It can also mean to conquer in battle by the spear-point. **Likeness**; <note>original: "dikelon"</note> properly refers to a statue resembling Zeus.

<margin>
In an extended sense, this term refers to any likeness or image, as we use it today. We also call mockers "Dikelistai"—those who imitate someone else in order to ridicule them.
</margin>

->NEXT WAS FASHIONED DEEP-TRESSED CYTHEREIA,<-
-><note>Cythereia is a common epithet for Aphrodite, the goddess of love.</note><-
->RESTRAINING THE SWIFT SHIELD OF ARES; AND FROM HER SHOULDER<-
->THE FASTENING OF HER TUNIC HAD LOOSENED OVER HER LEFT FOREARM<-
->BENEATH HER BREAST; AND OPPOSITE HER, QUITE CLEARLY,<-
->A LIKENESS APPEARED IN THE BRONZE SHIELD TO BE SEEN.<-
->AND THERE WAS A SHAGGY PASTURE FOR CATTLE, AND AROUND THE COWS<-
->THE TELEBOANS FOUGHT, AND THE SONS OF ELECTRYON.<-

The poet says that in the shield, which was made of bronze, a similar form of the goddess appeared. To show that reflections occurred in the polished metal, he describes how, as Aphrodite’s shoulder was bared down to her breast, her image was reflected on the opposite side because the shield's surface was so smooth. **Among the cattle**; Taphos is one of the Echinades islands. It was inhabited by the Teleboans, who previously lived in Acarnania; they were the most pirate-like men of that era. Coming to Argos, they drove away the cattle of Electryon, who was the father of Alcmene <note>the mother of Heracles</note>. In the battle that followed, both Electryon and his sons were killed. Because of this, Alcmene moved away and announced she would marry whoever avenged her father’s murder. Amphitryon, having taken that vengeance, married her. This story is told clearly in Hesiod; and the historian Herodorus <note>a mythographer from the late 5th century BCE</note> records regarding the battle that from Perseus and Andromeda, four sons were born...

<meta>This page continues the description of the mythological scenes embroidered upon Jason’s mantle. Following the depiction of Aphrodite with the shield of Ares, the text moves to a violent scene involving the sons of Electryon and the subsequent chariot race of Pelops, which established the Pelopid dynasty.</meta>

Alcaeus, Sthenelus, Mestor, and Electryon <note>These were the sons of the hero Perseus and Andromeda.</note> held the kingdom in common after the death of Perseus. Mestor’s daughter was Hippothoe; she and Poseidon <note>The god of the sea</note> were the parents of Pterelaus. Pterelaus was the father of Teleboas and Taphos. Some say Pterelaus was actually the son of Teleboas. From them came the children known as the Teleboans. They came to demand from Electryon the property belonging to their grandmother Hippothoe. When the sons of Electryon stood against them, they were killed by the Teleboans. Teleboas and Taphos were the sons of Pterelaus, and the island <note>The island of Taphos in the Ionian Sea</note> was named after Taphos.

<margin>
The Teleboans are the same as the Taphians. Their name means "those who dwell far off" <note>original: "tele oikountes"</note>. They drove away the cattle from Argos, or they took their name from Teleboas, the son of King Pterelaus.
</margin>

**Some were fighting back, while others sought to plunder—**
**The Taphian pirates; and with their blood the dewy meadow**
**Was drenched. The many were overpowering the few herdsmen.**
**And in the fabric two chariots were fashioned, as if competing.**
**The one in front was guided by Pelops, who shook the reins;**
**And beside him was Hippodamia as his passenger.**

Taphos was the brother of Teleboas, and the island is named for him. **To plunder** <note>original: "amersai"</note> means to deprive someone of something. **Competing** <note>original: "derionton"</note> means struggling in a contest. 

For Oenomaus—who was the son of Ares and Harpinne (the daughter of Asopus), or perhaps Eurythoe (the daughter of Danaus)—had a daughter named Hippodamia. Having received an oracle that he would be killed by his own son-in-law, he refused to give her in marriage unless a suitor could defeat him in a chariot race. The starting point for the contestants was the river Cladeus, and the finish line was the Isthmus of Corinth. He killed sixteen suitors in this way, as the poet Pindar records. 

When Pelops arrived for the contest, he brought horses given to him by Poseidon. Hippodamia fell in love with Pelops and persuaded Myrtilus—the son of Hermes and the chariot-builder and driver for Oenomaus—to help him. Myrtilus inserted a waxen linchpin <note>original: "embolon"</note> into the end of the chariot’s axle, or perhaps he replaced the metal bolt entirely, as the historian Pherecydes relates. Because of this, Oenomaus was thrown from the wheel as it spun and died. Thus, Pelops took Hippodamia as his wife. 

The names of Oenomaus's horses were Philla and Harpippa. Myrtilus was the son of Hermes and either Phaethousa (one of the daughters of Danaus) or Myrto (one of the Amazons). Regarding the term **passenger** <note>original: "parabatis," literally "one who stands beside"</note>: this does not mean she was actually beside him during the heat of the race, but rather that the artist wanted to show both the race and the victory together in a single image.

That Tityos was indeed great, Homer also says: "he lay stretched over nine plethra" <note>A plethron was approximately 100 feet; this suggests Tityos covered nearly 900 feet of ground.</note>. <meta>This page continues the analysis of Jason’s mantle, specifically interpreting the allegorical meaning behind the embroidered scenes. ...to which the poet did not use the proper name, but called her "mother" according to her nature, saying: "In which was Phrixus the Minyan." Then he shows all things that happen in cities, both loves and wars; for this is what he intends by the image of Aphrodite bearing weapons. Violence and battles are shown through the history of the Taphians <note>A legendary people of the islands near Acarnania, often associated with piracy</note>, and marriages through the labors of Pelops. He shows impiety and punishment by a superior power through the figure of Tityos. Plots, snares, good encounters, and unexpected salvation are shown through the story of Phrixus. In short, he poetically expressed almost everything that happens in human societies through the imagery of the cloak. He says the cloak is a gift from Athena because the world was created by divine wisdom <note>original: "phroneseos"</note>. Furthermore, none of the things practiced by men within the world could be done correctly without wisdom. The followers of Aristarchus <note>A famous Homeric scholar and librarian at Alexandria</note> have different spellings for such things, as Heracleon says in his commentary on the *Iliad*. "Meanwhile, taking it from the chest": then, sitting by the maiden, he handles the maidenly gifts.

CYPRIS <note>Aphrodite, the goddess of love, often called "the Cyprian"</note> WAS PREPARED, WHO CAST A SOUL-DESTROYING INFATUATION <note>original: *atē*; a divinely sent delusion or ruin</note> UPON THEM.

**In case ever again** <note>original: *Eiké pot' autis*</note>: the conjunction "and" is redundant here. The sense of the passage is: "we endured for a long time [to see] if they would repent." In order to avoid accusing the women of mere jealousy or lack of self-control, the poet says they reflected "sweetly" <note>bittersweetly</note> on their suffering. **And widowed mothers beside them**: so as not to accuse the young maidens of wandering about for lewd reasons, he says they were in distress because of their widowed mothers and were caring for them. The word **wandered** <note>original: *alālēnto*</note> applies to both the mothers and the daughters. In another sense, it means that none of us were looking toward marriage; for we were occupied with the needs of our mothers and the insults they received, which taught us what our own futures would be. **Nor did a father**: to create a greater sense of pity and emphasis, the poet uses natural family titles <note>e.g., father, daughter, mother</note> throughout this section.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Book 1 of Apollonius Rhodius's Argonautica. Wondrous men! <note>original: *Daimonioi* — a term of address that can mean "divinely inspired" but here carries a tone of sharp, ironic reproach</note> These words are appropriate to the dignity of heroes. Artfully and proportionately, he does not rebuke just one person, but everyone. And first, he reproaches them for their lack of self-control before declaring what is beneficial. Among the natural philosophers <note>the *physikoia*, or those who interpret myths as allegories for natural or psychological forces</note>, Heracles is taken to represent intelligence <term>synesis; the ability to grasp the reality of a situation</term> and strength. So the account shows that the heroes, having yielded to pleasure, recover themselves through reason. The meaning is: "O blessed ones! We are kept away from our [kin]..."

...from which we are kept away from our fatherland. Since such people were punished with exile from their fatherland for a year on account of blood-guilt <note>original: *emiaiaia* — refers to the legal tradition where a person guilty of involuntary homicide was exiled for a single year to be purified</note>. "Having scorned the city-women": he specifically used the term "city-women" <note>original: *politidas* — women who share the same civic status</note>. As if to say: "Having rejected the women of our own land, we have come to live with foreigners." And he says this as if they fled from their beauty. For perhaps it was true that the women in Lemnos happened to be more beautiful. "Famous" <note>original: *Eukleeis*</note>: glorious. And for this reason, he insults them. For he knows that each of them came on this voyage for sweet glory, but they lost it because they lingered for so long. "Cooped up for a long time": here too, he wisely and skillfully blames the passage of time. For while neglecting their labor for a little while was open to forgiveness, doing so for a long time was unbearable for any man who has abandoned his duty. As the saying goes: "In everything there is satiety" <note>A common Greek proverb meaning that even good things become tiresome or excessive over time</note>.

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary on the first book of Apollonius Rhodius's Argonautica. Having previously discussed Heracles's harsh lecture to the Argonauts, the commentator now examines the grammatical technicalities of Heracles's final command and the famous "bee simile" that describes the women of Lemnos rushing to say goodbye to the departing heroes.</meta>

"Let us each go back to our own [homes/places]." <note>original: *Iomen autis hekastoi epi sphea* — Argonautica 1.883</note> The word "their own" <note>original: *sphea*</note> is not used properly here. For the word *sphea* is equivalent to a third-person usage. He should have said, "Let us each go back to **our own**" <note>original: *emethera*</note>. This is because of the proper conjugation of the persons: "ours," "yours," "theirs." Similarly for "ours," "yours"... "He will fill with men" <note>original: *esandrōsē*</note>; that is, he will fill it with men in a heroic fashion. 
**Lilies.** <note>original: *Leiria*</note> Generally, all flowers are called *leiria*. But specifically, it refers to the flower called the lily. This is what

<margin>
Theophrastus, in 
his work *On 
Plants*, says 
is the narcissus. 
But others say 
it is the lily. 
**Symbleidos.** 
They call the 
caves in which 
bees mold their 
wax *symbleidas* 
[hives].
</margin>

> ...TO ALL IT WAS MANNED, AND A GREAT FOUNDATION WAS REACHED. 
> AS HE REBUKED THE CROWD. AND NO ONE THEN DARED 
> TO HOLD THEIR EYES AGAINST HIM, NOR TO SPEAK IN RESPONSE. 
> BUT JUST AS THEY WERE GATHERED, THEY PREPARED TO GO 
> IN HASTE. AND THE WOMEN RAN TO THEM LIKE BEES, 
> AS WHEN BEAUTIFUL LILIES ARE BUZZED AROUND BY BEES 
> POURING OUT FROM A ROCKY HIVE. AND AROUND THEM THE DEWY 
> MEADOW REJOICES. AND THEY PLUCK THE SWEET 
> FRUIT, NOW ONE, NOW ANOTHER, FLITTING ABOUT; SO THEN THEY...

...therefore, of a rock in which they make honey in the mountains, which has the character of a beehive <term>symblos; a hollow place or vessel used as a hive</term>. 
**Now one, now another.** This follows the saying of Isocrates: "For just as we see the bee settling on all the blossoms, but collecting what is useful from each, so also should those seeking <insert>an education</insert>." 
**So then they.** This refers to the Lemnian women. However, the simile is not strictly accurate, nor does it fit in every detail. For the poet seems to liken the women to bees, the heroes to flowers, and the city to a hollow hive. But would not the remaining parts be a mismatch? Through these words, he says the meadow rejoices and delights, and yet the city is in grief. He also uses the word "wailing." Furthermore, it is a mismatch to say they "pluck the sweet fruit, now one, now another." For surely each of the women will not be taking [a fruit] from both of the heroes. These details were better suited to the first meeting and union. 
**Alternatively:** To those who find fault with the simile, one must say that not everything mentioned in a comparison must fit the subjects at hand; some parts of the simile are included for the clarity of the events, while others are for beauty and description <term>ekphrasis; a vivid, often poetic, description of a scene or work of art</term> alone.

**"Better than my heart"** <note>original: *Emēthen perithymon areiō*</note>: The sense is: "You should hold a better soul and opinion concerning me," despite our joking about our fatherland; for we are not in such a state as to have abandoned our own land to migrate to another. **"By the will of Pelias"** <note>original: *Peliao hekēti*</note>: This means: "It is because of Pelias that I must inhabit the land of Hellas"—referring here to Thessaly. **Kindly** <note>original: *endykes*</note>: That which, after much hardship, becomes pleasant and sweet. <meta>This page transitions from the Argonauts' departure from Lemnos to their arrival at Samothrace. Zeus fathered children: Dardanus, who settled in Troy and whom the locals say is called the "ancestral founder" <note>original: *genuarchēn*</note>, and Eetion, whom they also call Iasion. They say that Iasion was struck by lightning for committing an outrage against a statue of Demeter. He had a sister <note>original: *rhytin*, likely a scribal error for *adelphēn*</note> named Harmonia, whom Cadmus took as his wife. From her mother, Electra, he named the "Electran Gates" of Thebes. Hellanicus records this in the first book of his *Troica* <note>A history of Troy</note>, as does Idomeneus in...

<margin>
...the first book of the *Troica*. "Unutterable" <note>original: *arrhēktous*</note> he says instead of "the secret rites"; those celebrated in Samothrace; which if...
</margin>

> They beat the water with long oars powerfully;
> At dawn, by the mountain's commands, they reached
> The island of Electra, daughter of Atlas, so that learning
> The unutterable laws through holy initiations,
> They might sail more safely over the chilling sea.

...one is initiated into these, they are saved during storms at sea. They say that Odysseus, too, having been initiated in Samothrace, used the veil [of the sea-goddess Leucothea] in place of a headband <note>original: *tainia*; a ritual headband worn by initiates</note>. For those who have been initiated tie purple bands around their waists. They also say that Agamemnon, having been initiated and being in great turmoil at Troy due to the instability of the leaders, quelled the disturbance while wearing a purple garment.

In Samothrace, people are initiated into the mysteries of the <term>Kabeiroi</term> <note>Mysterious chthonic deities of the underworld and fertility</note>, whose names Mnaseas provides. They are four in number: Axieros, Axiokersa, Axiokersos. Axieros is Demeter; Axiokersa is Persephone; and Axiokersos is Hades. The fourth added to these is Kasmilos, who is Hermes, as Dionysodorus records. 

Athenion, however, says that Iasion and Dardanus were born to Zeus and Electra. The Kabeiroi seem to be named after the "Kabeiroi Mountains" in Phrygia <note>Modern-day Turkey</note>, since they were brought from there. Others say there were originally only two Kabeiroi: the elder being Zeus and the younger being Dionysus. 

Samothrace was formerly called Leukosia, as Aristotle records in his *Constitution of Samothrace*. Later, it was named Samos after Saos, the son of Hermes and Rhene, through the insertion of the letter 'm'. When Thracians settled the island, it was called Samothrace <note>literally "Samos of Thrace"</note>. 

**"More safely"** <note>original: *sōoteroi*</note>: meaning with less danger. For it is said that those initiated there are heard in whatever they pray for, as Aristophanes says: "Therefore, if any of you happen to have been initiated in Samothrace, now is a good time to pray." For those who know the mysteries seem to be saved more effectively.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Argonauts' visit to Samothrace. "Of these things I shall speak no further" <note>original: *Tōn men et' ou proterō*</note>: The word "further" indicates moving forward; as in Homer, "nor did the ships go further for me." Here it is used figuratively regarding his speech. The meaning is this: "I will say nothing more about these matters." Instead, let the island be favored, and let the gods whose mysteries these are be favored. For it is not proper for us to speak of them.

<margin>
**To speak of the Secret Rites** <note>original: *Orgia*</note>: The mysteries; named so from the "warding off" <note>original: *eirgein*</note> of the uninitiated. Or, those things that take place in "moist places" <note>original: *orgasin*</note>. For "orgades" are places that are overgrown and damp. **The Black** <note>original: *Melanos*</note>: The "Black Sea" <note>The Euxine or the Hellespont region</note> is so called as we know. Eudoxus says this in the second book of his *Circuit of the Earth*.

**Commentary:** They say that this is the same as the Sarpedonian rock. Regarding why it is called the "Black Sea": Homer mentions the "black northern sea," and it was named either after the "black" Phrixus who fell into it, or after a river called "Black" <note>original: *Melas*</note> that flows there. **The land of the Thracians**: This was on the right hand. **The land across** <note>original: *Peraiēn*</note>: This refers to the land lying opposite; for Imbros is directly across from Thrace. Rhoiteion is also a silent promontory of Ilium <note>Troy</note>. **Abarnis**: Abarnis is a city of Lampsacus. It was named for the following reason: Aphrodite, having fallen in love with Dionysus, lay with him, and when he departed...

—who was in other respects deformed, and having an oversized member, he was called Priapus. When Aphrodite saw him, she did not think it right to take him up, loathing the child for his general ugliness and the indecency of his member. Because Aphrodite had "denied" <note>original: *aparnēthēnai*</note> the child there, the city was named Aparnis. Later, by shifting a letter <note>from P to B</note>, it was called Abarnis. In this Propontis, then, there is an island which later became a peninsula or possessed an isthmus. For every land jutting out into the sea is called an "isthmus" <note>the commentator uses this term broadly for a neck of land or peninsula</note>. Adjacent to this peninsula is Bear Mountain <note>original: *Arcton Oros*</note>, so called because they say the nurses of Zeus lived there and were transformed into bears; or because it is a deserted place named after the wild bears there; or because of the mountain’s height, appearing to reach the stars of the Bear <note>the constellation Ursa Major</note>. Certain wild Earth-born giants used to dwell there. But the peninsula and the isthmus were inhabited by the Doliones, over whom Cyzicus ruled.

The sequence [of the poem] is as follows: there is a certain high island in the Propontis, a short distance from Phrygia, lying against the land at the flow of the isthmus, above the Aesepus river, having shores on both sides. They call the mountain "Bear," and it is a peninsula upon which the city of the Cyzicenes is situated.

...and situated in the sea; it is a place possessing an isthmus. Then, he speaks with wonder at "how much" that isthmus roars as it is beaten by the waves. An isthmus is the name given to a place that has sea on both of its sides, as if it were a "pathway" <note>original: *isimos*, a play on the word *ienai*, "to go"</note>. It is called an *isthmus* because it is in a narrow place, which is also why the parts of the throat are called the *paristhmia* <note>the tonsils or "parts near the narrow passage"</note>. A "strait" <note>original: *porthmos*</note>, however, is a narrow sea that has land on both sides. **Covered**: meaning either "flowing down," "blown down," or "covered with plants." **Earthborn**: Herodorus also mentions this in his *History of the Argonauts*, noting that they fought against Heracles. So, the Earthborn giants lived near Cyzicus, while the Doliones lived near the isthmus. **And among them the hero son of Aeneus**: because Aeneus, being Thessalian by race, lived in Thessalonica. After marrying the daughter of Eusorus, the king of the Thracians, he fathered Aenetes, who is Cyzicus—from whom the city takes its name. But Akamas is the son of Eusorus, whom Homer mentions in the *Catalogue of Ships* <note>original: *Boiotia*, referring to the second book of the Iliad</note> as leading the Thracians along with Peiros. **Alternatively**: Cyzicus' father was Aeneus, the son of Apollo and Stilbe; the city was named after him. His daughter was Evantheia. He moved from Thessaly, where he used to live.

[Cyzicus] was leading the same life-age as Jason. The text is written as "recently upon him the down sprouted" <note>original: "harmoi g' hyp' ekeinō hypēntheueskon"</note>. This means "lately" or "recently." "They were sprouting" <note>original: "hypēnxanon"</note> means "they were blooming." The "down" <term>ioulos: a word with many meanings, starting here with the first growth of a beard</term> is the name for the first flowering and growth of the hair on the chin. However, Eratosthenes <note>a famous 3rd-century BC polymath and librarian at Alexandria</note> rendered it as the name of a song of the wool-workers, speaking thus in his *Hermes*: "Some worker girl led the way, upon the high gate, making flaxen threads, she sang the beautiful *ioulos* song." But Didymus <note>a prolific 1st-century BC scholar</note> says this is not so; rather, it is a hymn to Demeter <note>goddess of the harvest</note>, just as the "oupiggos" is a hymn to Artemis among the people of Troezen. For a "bundle" <note>original: "oulos" or "ioulos"</note> is the sheaf gathered from the handfuls of grain; and Demeter is sometimes called "Holos" <note>the Whole or Sheaf-Goddess</note>. Furthermore, *ioulos* is also the name of a many-footed living creature <note>a millipede or centipede</note>. For it has many feet on both sides like a "skolopendra." Theophrastus, in his letter to Phanias, also says this name is used, as it appears in the *Mute Satyrs* of Sophocles: "rolling like some many-footed *ioulos* donkey" <note>The translator notes this is an obscure comic comparison</note>. Allotted <note>original: "Memoreto"</note>: it had been assigned by fate <note>original: "ekeklērōto"</note> or "they held a portion of destiny." The grammatical construction is: "not yet was it fated for him to rejoice in children." The participle is used instead of the infinitive "to be fated." Undefiled <note>original: "Akeratos"</note>: meaning "childless" and "clean of birth-pains." This refers to Cleite, the daughter of Merops of Percote. Cyzicus's lineage was from a seer, as Deilochus and Ephorus record.

**Dindymon** is a mountain of Cyzicus sacred to Rhea. It is so called because "twin breasts"

**The Molded Harbor** 
<note>original: "Chytos Limen"</note>: 
A harbor in Cyzicus named thus because the Pelasgians attempted to "mound it up" <note>fill it with earth</note>, as Deilochus says. They did this out of hatred toward the Thessalians <note>the Argonauts' kin</note> by whom they had been driven out. But the poet says it was mounded up by the **Earthborn giants** <note>original: "Gegeneis"</note>, treating the whole matter poetically. 

Regarding the **Earthborn giants**, Deilochus says they were savage <term>hand-bellies<note>original: "cheirogastores"; a mythical race often depicted with multiple arms growing from their sides</note></term>. He says the Earthborn who plotted against the Argonauts were actually pirates. 

"Like jars" <note>original: "Amphoreas"</note>: some say this refers to them being broken open or split or "eaten away" by the sea. 

Theodorus says mythically that the Earthborn were turned against Heracles by the goddess Hera.

The myth claims they were born from the Nemean Lion <note>original: "Nemeaiou leontos"</note>; however, Lygnorus, in his writings concerning Cyzicus, identifies them as pirates. ...so that it might become a lightning-struck rock <note>original: "pagos keraunios"</note>.
"Others" <note>original: "Olloi"</note>: This form "Olloi" belongs to the younger Ionian dialect.
The word "surely" <note>original: "dethen"</note>: Sometimes used as a filler word, other times meaning "plainly" or "of course." Or perhaps the phrase is transposed; for the logical sequence is: "as the others, surely turning back, met them and engaged in slaughter."

**THEY BLOCKED THE MOUTH OF THE VAST HARBOR BELOW THE ROCK,**
**WATCHING LIKE SEA-BEASTS LURKING WITHIN AN AMBUSH.**

**LIFTED JAGGED ROCKS AND HURLED THEM.**
**FOR INDEED, THOSE TERRIBLE MONSTERS HAD BEEN REARED BY THE GODDESS**
**HERA, WIFE OF ZEUS, TO BE AN ORDEAL FOR HERACLES.**
**AND THEN THE OTHERS, SURELY RETURNING TO MEET THEM,**
**JOINED THE SLAUGHTER BEFORE THEY HAD EVEN ASCENDED THE LOOKOUT—**
**THESE WARLIKE HEROES AGAINST THE EARTHBORN. SOME WITH ARROWS,**
**OTHERS WITH SPEARS, THEY FACED THEM UNTIL THEY HAD SLAUGHTERED**
**ALL THOSE WHO RUSHED VIOLENTLY AND UNCEASINGLY AGAINST THEM.**
**AS WHEN WOODCUTTERS CAST LONG TIMBERS, NEWLY STRUCK BY AXES,**
**IN ROWS UPON THE SHORE OF THE SEA,**
**SO THAT, ONCE SOAKED, THEY MIGHT RECEIVE THE STURDY DOWELS,**

---

"Until they [slaughtered] all": They slaughtered them while they were being stirred up <note>original: "tarassomenous"</note> incessantly or unshakeably; or rather, opposing their strength, they destroyed them without pause. "As when long timbers": This comparison is fitting in every way and quite literal. He compares the giants to logs because of the "softness" of their bodies and because they lived in the mountains; he likewise compares the heroes to woodcutters. The phrase "so that, once soaked, they might receive the sturdy dowels": This refers to the practice on the shores, and for another reason: carpenters soak wood so they are spared greater labor; while working, they would drive in the wedges. In the same way, the heroes destroyed the giants so that, henceforth, the ascent of the mountain would be free of danger. "So that, once soaked": So that, being dampened, they might become receptive to the wedges <note>original: "sphēnon"</note>.

"In the narrow pass" <note>original: "Eni xunochē"</note>: meaning in the circumference or at the entrance of the harbor. "Diving their heads" <note>original: "Duptontes kephalas"</note>: instead of "sinking their heads." The author uses a continuous tense <term>paratatikon: the imperfect or progressive aspect</term> instead of a completed tense <term>syntelikon: the perfective aspect</term>, "having dived." This refers to them being cast down headfirst by the striking blows. To "dive" <term>duptein</term> means to sink, as seen in the poet Callimachus: "the divers <note>original: "duptai"</note> coming up from the sea." Earlier, Antimachus said:

**STORMS CARRIED THEM BACK BY FORCE, UNTIL THEY APPROACHED**
**ONCE AGAIN THE DECEPTIVE SHORES OF THE EUXINE. AND SO THEY DISEMBARKED**
**THAT VERY NIGHT. AND THIS IS STILL CALLED THE HOLY ROCK,**
**WHERE THEY, RUSHING FORTH, CAST THE SHIP’S CABLES.**

"But at night," the breath of the wind no longer remained the same. "Instead, storms" <note>original: "thuellai"</note>: these are the wintry blasts and tempests. Hence, Homer treats "storms" and "snatchers" <note>original: "harpyiai"</note> as synonyms for tempestuous winds; the name is derived from "snatching" <note>original: "harpazein"</note>. For instance: "the storms <note>original: "thuellai"</note> snatched up the daughters of Pandareus." And then: "meanwhile the snatchers <note>original: "harpyiai"</note> carried off the girls," as if they were the same thing. The one name comes from "snatching," and the other from "rushing" <note>original: "thuein"</note>, which means to move with violence. He used the word "forcibly" <note>original: "harpagdēn"</note> from "snatching," just as "carried" <note>original: "phoradēn"</note> comes from "carrying," and "rushing" <note>original: "aigdēn"</note> comes from "darting." "And they disembarked": they went out and approached the "deceptive" shores again. By "deceptive" <note>original: "euxinoisin"</note>, he speaks as if he himself is suffering at the events that occurred. "It is called Holy": according to local tradition. For the things...

They say that other afflictions are "holy" and "good" out of euphemism <note>Using a mild or positive word to describe something unpleasant.</note>; just as they call the Furies the "Eumenides" <note>original: "Eumenidas" - meaning 'The Kindly Ones'</note> and infectious leprosy "holy." Of the Macrianes, those called Macrians are colonists of the Euboeans. From this, they were called Macrianes, for Euboea was also called Macris.

<margin>
He called it Pelasgian because Euboea is a neighboring land to the Peloponnese. Or, it was previously called Pelasgia. The Macrianes were neighbors of the Doliones.

They say the Macrians are a "short-armed" <note>original: "bracheirōn"</note> nation who are always at war with the Cyzicenians. Others say they are called Macrianes because <unclear>it lies flat</unclear> among the long-headed people <note>original: "makrokephaloi"</note>, just as "hook-nosed" <note>original: "grypous"</note> is a trait among the Persians. He called it a "Pelasgian war" <note>original: "Pelasgikon area"</note> of the Macrianes because they are colonists of the Euboeans, and Euboea lies near the Peloponnese, which was called Pelasgis in ancient times. "And he dashed together" <note>original: "Sun d’ elasen"</note>: the little 'o' marks a new paragraph. They joined together in fury; spears and the spirit of men. "Which in the thickets" <note>original: "Ēt’ eni thamnois"</note>: referring to the stalks of the trees based on their position. "A thicket of long-leafed olive grew." These lines are also drawn from Homer: "He raged like Ares the spear-brandisher or as a destructive fire rages in the mountains in the deep recesses of a thick wood." "Furious" <term>zamenēs: exceedingly strong</term>. The prefix "za-" is used for intensification <term>epitasin</term>, as in "very wealthy" <note>original: "zaplytos"</note>, "very angry" <note>original: "zakotos"</note>, or "very holy" <note>original: "zatheos"</note>. ...having: and it is called **aphlaston** by association or by contradiction <note>original: "antiphrasin"</note>, since it is actually "easily crushed" <note>a Greek pun: *a-phlaston* means "un-crushable," but the commentator notes it is actually fragile wood</note>. Therefore, the **aphlaston** is a small plank at the stern. **For from her the winds.** From this Rhea <note>the Mother of the Gods</note>; both earth and sea and sky are held together. For the natural philosophers interpret her as **Universal Harmony** <note>original: "pantarmo-synēn"</note>. And they etymologize her name from the word "to flow" <note>original: "rhein," a common ancient pun connecting the goddess Rhea to the flow of nature</note> always and creating currents. And naturally they say her husband is **Cronus**, as if he were **Chronos** <note>Time</note>, by the change of a single letter. They associate this with the order of the elements; by necessity, Time leads the way. Allegorically, they say these are the fathers of the sea, heavenly, and earthly gods. For after the placement and binding of the elements, it happened that men learned of and honored the divine powers and the differences between the gods. The word **pepeirētai** <note>original: "pepeirētai"</note> is used instead of "is held together" or "they are contained."

The **Bosporus** <note>literally "Cow-Crossing"</note> is the narrow part of the Propontis <note>the Sea of Marmara</note>, so named after the cow, **Io**, who swam across it. **"And on the other side"** refers to the continent of Europe, for Mysia and the Aesepus are in Asia. He speaks of another region, the Troad, through which the Aesepus flows, separating it from Mysia. Homer also mentions the Granicus and the Aesepus. The Troad, beginning from Great Mysia, ends at the Aesepus. Dolionia and Phrygia begin at the Aesepus and end at the Rhyndacus river. There are two Mysias: the European and the Asian. It was the hills of Asian Mysia that appeared to the Argonauts. **"And the Nepeian plain."** The Nepeian plain is around Cyzicus; Callimachus also mentions it in his poem *Hecale*.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on Apollonius Rhodius’s epic poem, the *Argonautica*. The Argonauts have ascended Mount Dindymus to appease the goddess Rhea. The text discusses the geographical locations mentioned in the poem and provides a detailed breakdown of the vocabulary used to describe the creation of a cult statue for the goddess. The catchword "ζιι" at the bottom of the previous page matches the starting content here.</meta>

...Neseian or the famous Adrasteia. Regarding "Neseian," Dionysius of Miletus says it is a plain in Mysia. He relates that the king of the Mysians had a daughter by Iasus <note>A mythical king of Argos or Arcadia</note> named Olympus Neseia, who was pregnant. She settled in this plain, which is now called the Nepeian plain. However, Apollodorus <note>A famous Athenian scholar and mythographer</note> claims the Neseian plain is in Phrygia. Callimachus says in his *Commentaries* that it is Nemesis <note>The goddess of retribution</note> who possesses the plain.

> THERE REMAINED A STURDY STUMP OF A VINE, A VERY OLD TREE GROWING IN THE WOODS.
> THIS THEY CUT DOWN TO BE A SACRED IMAGE <note>original: "bretas"</note> OF THE MOUNTAIN GODDESS. 
> ARGOS CARVED IT SKILLFULLY. AND THEN THEY SET IT UP ON A RUGGED HILL, 
> BENEATH THE HIGHEST OAK TREES, WHICH OF ALL TREES ARE ROOTED THE DEEPEST. 
> NEARBY THEY HEAPED UP AN ALTAR OF PEBBLES; 
> AND CROWNING THEMSELVES WITH OAK LEAVES, THEY ATTENDED TO THE SACRIFICE.

<column-break/>

There is also a city called Adrasteia, named after its founder. Apollonius mentions both the city and the plain, for he says "the city and the Neseian plain of Adrasteia." Homer also mentions the city: "those who held Adrasteia" <note>A reference to the *Iliad*, book 2</note>. 

**There remained a sturdy...** 
**Stump** <note>original: "stypos"</note> refers to the base and the stem, from which the word "to beat with a stick" <note>original: "apostypazon"</note> is derived. 

**Sacred Image** <note>original: "bretas"</note> refers to a figure resembling a mortal <note>original: "brotōi"</note> and the movement of human beings. Regarding this, he says the wooden statue <note>original: "xoanon"</note> of the Mother of the Gods <note>Rhea</note> was made of vine wood, perhaps because the vine is sacred to Rhea. 

**Down to the roots** <note>original: "prochnu"</note> means completely. 
**Old tree** <note>original: "gerandryon"</note> means an ancient trunk. 
**On a hill.** On the protruding mountain-peak. 
**Pebbles.** <note>original: "cherados"</note> A collection of small stones, specifically those small enough to be picked up one by one in the hand, which Homer calls "hand-stones" <note>original: "chermadia"</note>. The phrase "built an altar" refers to the construction of the altar itself. Alternatively, "shingle" <note>original: "cheradon"</note> is what they call small heaps of stones. Demetrius of Skepsis <note>A grammarian known for his commentary on the Trojan catalog in the *Iliad*</note> says this is the dialect of the Apollonians in the Pontus. Sappho also mentions it: "do not stir the pebbles." And Homer: "having poured out plenty of pebbles." "Pebbles" refers to the heap of stones; for the construction of the altar, they piled up stones. 

**With oak leaves.** Fittingly, the oak is also sacred to Rhea, as Apollodorus says in his work *On the Gods*. He says they crown themselves with oak leaves because this tree is dedicated to the goddess, as it was the first tree to be useful for both shelter and roofing.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on Apollonius Rhodius’s *Argonautica*. Following the previous discussion of the Neseian plain and the carving of the sacred image (bretas) of Rhea, the text now focuses on the specific titles of the goddess and her supernatural attendants, the Idaean Dactyls.</meta>

**Dindymian** <note>original: "Dindymikēn"</note>: this refers to the goddess honored on Mount Dindymus, whom they invoke and supplicate. "Dweller of Phrygia, Titias together with her..." Concerning those called the **Idaean Dactyls** <note>literally "The Fingers of Mount Ida," a group of mythical mountain-dwelling craftsmen, smiths, and magicians</note>, they say these were the first attendants and companions to the Mother of the Gods. This follows Menander, who says that those being initiated into the mysteries, when they sacrifice to Rhea, offer a preliminary sacrifice to Titias and Cyllenus. They say these figures are the **Guides of Fate** <note>original: "moiragetai"</note> among the Idaean Dactyls and attendants to the Mother of the Gods.

->INVOKING THE MOTHER OF DINDYMUS, THE MANY-TITLED MISTRESS.<-
->DWELLER OF PHRYGIA, AND WITH HER TITIAS AND CYLLENUS.<-
->WHO ALONE AMONG MANY ARE THE GUIDES OF FATE, AND THE ATTENDANTS<-
->OF THE IDAEAN MOTHER THEY ARE CALLED, AS MANY AS THERE ARE<-
->IDAEAN DACTYLS OF CRETE, WHOM ONCE THE NYMPH...<-

<margin>
Callistratus says in the second book of his work *On Heracleia* concerning Titias: "Titias was a local hero; whom some..."
</margin>
...some mythologize as a son of Zeus, while others say he was the eldest of the children of Mariandynus the Cimmerian <note>The legendary ancestor of the Mariandynians, a people in Bithynia</note>. It was because of him especially that the nation increased and was led toward prosperity. Promachidas also speaks about who Titias was in his works *On Heracleia*. So too does Theophanes, noting that he was deified by the Mariandynians. The story that a certain nymph named Anchiale created the Idaean Dactyls by clutching the earth of the Idaean land is taken from Stesimbrotus. It is said they were called **Dactyls** <note>Fingers</note> because they "fostered" <note>original: "euthēnai," an ancient play on words suggesting they handled the child with their fingers</note> the infant Zeus with their hands. Sophocles, however, calls them Phrygians in his play *The Mute Satyrs*.

**Idaean Dactyls**: Some say there are five males and six females; the males are on the right and the females on the left. Pherecydes, however, says there are twenty on the right and thirty-two on the left <note>original: "euōnymous," literally "the well-named" ones, a common ancient euphemism used for the unlucky left side</note>. They were said to be **sorcerers** <note>original: "goētes"</note> and masters of potions, and are called the first to work with iron and the first to become miners. They were named after their mother, Ida. According to Pherecydes, the ones on the left are the sorcerers, while those on the right are the ones who "undo" or release spells, as Hellanicus says. Others claim they were called Idaean Dactyls because they met Rhea on Mount Ida and either greeted her with their voices <note>a play on the Greek word "dexiousthai," to greet or offer the right hand</note> or touched her fingers <note>original: "daktylōn"</note>. As Mnaseas says in the first book of *On Asia*, the Idaean Dactyls are named after their father Dactylus and their mother Ida. The author of the *Phoronis* <note>An early, largely lost Greek epic poem centered on the hero Phoroneus</note> writes the following: "There the Idaean sorcerers, Phrygian men of the mountains, had their dwelling: Kelmis, Damnameneus the Great, and the overweening Akmon; skillful servants of the mountain goddess Adrasteia."

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on Apollonius Rhodius’s *Argonautica*, Book 1. Having introduced the Idaean Dactyls as attendants of the Mother of the Gods, the text now details their origin in the Dictaean cave of Crete and the ritual dances performed by the Argonauts to drown out the mourning cries of the Doliones.</meta>

They were the first to find the art of wily Hephaestus <note>The god of fire and smithing</note> in the glens of the Berecynthians—the visible iron. They brought it to the fire and displayed a distinguished work. **Dictaean** <note>original: "Diktaion"</note>: This refers to the Cretan cave. For Dicte is a mountain in Crete. **Brought forth** <note>original: "eblastēsen"</note>: used here instead of "gave birth." **Grasping** <note>original: "draxamenē"</note>: It is the custom for women in labor to take hold of nearby objects and support themselves against the pains; just as Leto <note>Mother of Apollo and Artemis</note> took hold of the palm tree. However, the poet should have said "Oaxian" <note>referring to the Oaxes river in Crete</note>.

<margin>
The letter *iota* was added. **Eryolas** <note>appeasing invocations</note>: This word has been read in various ways, but the grave accent is the prevailing pronunciation. **Of Orthos** <note>original: "Orthēos"</note>: this concerns the land; but according to the "direct" <note>original: "orthēōs"</note> encouragement. This is as if he were the leader of the dance. **Betarmon** <note>a measured tread or dance</note>: the poet provides the suitable step for the dance.
</margin>

->ANCHIALE, WITHIN THE DICTAEAN CAVE, GRASPING THE OAXIAN EARTH<-
->WITH BOTH HANDS, BROUGHT FORTH THE DACTYLS.<-
->AND WITH MANY PRAYERS THE SON OF AESON <note>Jason</note> INVOKED HER<-
->WITH APPEASING SUPPLICATIONS, POURING LIBATIONS UPON THE BLAZING<-
->SACRIFICES. AT THE SAME TIME THE YOUNG MEN, AT THE BIDDING OF ORTHOS,<-
->LEAPING, DANCED THE MEASURED ARMED DANCE<-
->AND CLASHED THEIR SHIELDS WITH SWORDS, SO THAT THE ILL-OMENED CRY<-
->MIGHT BE DISPERSED THROUGH THE AIR. WHICH THE PEOPLE STILL<-
->UTTERED IN GRIEF FOR THE KING. HENCEFORTH FOREVER<-
->THE PHRYGIANS PROPITIATE RHEA WITH THE BULL-ROARER AND THE DRUM.<-
->AND THE GODDESS ANTAIA TURNED HER MIND TO THE PIOUS OFFERINGS.<-
->AND THE FITTING SIGNS APPEARED.<-

...the suitable step for it. He is now speaking of the **Pyrrhic dance** <note>A traditional Greek war dance performed in full armor</note>. The following part means they danced, clashing their shields with swords because the death of King Cyzicus was still being mourned by the Doliones <note>The local people of Cyzicus who were accidentally attacked by the Argonauts</note>. This was done so that, while the sacrifice was taking place, no ill-omened sound of mourning would be carried up to the gods. This is why the Phrygians still propitiate Rhea with cymbals and drums. The **Rhombos** <note>literally "bull-roarer"</note> is a small wheel or piece of wood that they spin by striking it with thongs, and in this way they produce a roaring sound. Some call the instrument itself a *rhombos*, including the playwright Eupolis in his play *The Baptae*, and the scholar Didymus. **Antaia**: Rhea is called by this title because she was "opposite" <note>original: "enantia"</note> or hostile to the Telchines <note>mythical smiths and sorcerers</note>. However, some say *Antaia* means "easy-to-heal" or "easy-to-reach." **Signs appeared**: by this phrase the poet means nothing other than the nature of the goddess. Those who study nature <note>the "physikoi" or natural philosophers</note> say she is the same as the Earth. The sign of her favor was that the trees became fruitful and the grass grew spontaneously.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary and the primary text of Apollonius Rhodius’s *Argonautica*, Book 1. After the Argonauts perform the armed dance for the goddess Rhea, the text describes the miraculous signs of her favor—the blooming of the earth and the creation of a new spring—before the heroes set sail once more from the land of the Doliones.</meta>

**Of tender** <note>original: "tereinēs"</note>: This refers to that which is soft and green. **Lairs** <note>original: "elyous"</note>: This refers to the resting places of wild beasts. **Thickets** <note>original: "xylokhous"</note>: This refers to wooded places in the mountains. This passage uses a **transposition** <note>term: hyperbaton; a figure of speech where the natural order of words is changed for emphasis</note>: "leaving behind both lairs and thickets." Through many details, the poet presents the miracle: because the earth was "thirsty" <note>dry/parched</note>, and because the water was not merely a small amount but was given up in an unceasing flow. The word **to dwell** <note>original: "naien"</note> is not used well here.

<margin>
Written <note>as a variant</note> without the letter *iota*: **to flow** <note>original: "naein"</note>, so that it may be used with force as in Homer: "I see all things flowing." The syntax is by **transposition** <note>term: metathesis; a shifting of word order</note>, like the phrase "the earth flowed with blood" instead of "blood flowed in the earth." Or, the word "to flow" should be taken as meaning "flowing down," so that the mountain Dindymon was "flowing down with waters." **Burst forth** <note>original: "anebrakhthē"</note>: used instead of "was given up." **Thirsty** <note>original: "dipsas"</note>: signifies the dry land. Here he seems to call Cyzicus an island. **Storm-footed** <note>original: "aellopodas"</note>: refers to those who are swift. The word **reached** <note>original: "kikhon"</note> is used instead of "overtook." **With violent breezes** <note>original: "zakhreēsin aurais"</note>: meaning those that weigh heavily and blow greatly. Properly, the word *zakhreēs* refers to something done violently with the hands; the word is formed from "hands" <note>Greek: kheiras</note> and the intensive prefix *za-*. The word **they rested** <note>original: "metelōpheon"</note> is used instead of "they ceased."
</margin>

->THE TREES INDEED SHED FRUIT BEYOND MEASURE. AND AROUND THEIR FEET,<-
->THE EARTH OF ITS OWN ACCORD BROUGHT FORTH FLOWERS OF TENDER GRASS.<-
->AND THE WILD BEASTS, LEAVING THEIR LAIRS AND THICKETS,<-
->CAME FORWARD WAGGING THEIR TAILS. AND SHE ALSO<-
->PERFORMED ANOTHER MIRACLE; FOR NEVER BEFORE DID WATER FLOW<-
->ON DINDYMON. BUT THEN FOR THEM IT BURST FORTH FROM THE THIRSTY PEAK<-
->UNCEASINGLY. AND MEN OF LATER TIMES CALL THAT STREAM<-
->THE JASONIAN SPRING.<-
->AND THEN THEY SET A FEAST FOR THE GODDESS ON THE MOUNTAIN OF BEARS,<-
->SINGING OF RHEA, THE MUCH-REVERED. BUT AT DAWN,<-
->WHEN THE WINDS CEASED, THEY LEFT THE ISLAND BY ROWING.<-
->THEN STRIFE STIRRED EACH OF THE HEROES,<-
->TO SEE WHO WOULD BE THE LAST TO STOP ROWING. FOR THE WINDLESS AIR<-
->SMOOTHED THE EDDIES, AND CALMED THE SURGE OF THE SEA;<-
->TRUSTING IN THE CALM, THEY DROVE THE SHIP FORWARD<-
->BY MIGHT. NOT EVEN THE STORM-FOOTED HORSES OF POSEIDON<-
->COULD HAVE OVERTAKEN THE SHIP AS IT SPED THROUGH THE SEA.<-
->YET WHEN THE SURGE WAS STIRRED BY VIOLENT BREEZES,<-
->WHICH RISE UP FROM RIVERS IN THE COOL OF EVENING,<-
->THEY WERE WEARIED. AND INDEED THEY RESTED. BUT HE...<-

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary on Apollonius Rhodius’s Argonautica, specifically focusing on Hercules’s immense strength as he rows the Argo and the geographical landmarks the Argonauts pass as they reach the territory of the Mysians and the river Rhyndacus.</meta>

**He was dragging** <note>original: "ephelketo"</note>: [Used] in regards to <gloss>the</gloss> [attainment of] <gloss>com-</gloss> complete self-sufficiency and the overcoming of the waves; the word **he was dragging** was used with even greater emphasis. This is just as Callimachus says regarding the captured Bull: "nor did the slow traveler follow." **Rhyndacian** <note>original: "Rhyndakidas"</note>: Rhyndacus is a place in Phrygia mentioned by Bacchylides. In truth, it is the tomb of Briareus <note>A hundred-handed giant from Greek mythology</note> located at the entrance. Callimachus provides a history of the river in his [work]

# WITH ALL THEIR MIGHT HE DRAGGED THEM ALONG AS THEY LABORED BY THE STRENGTH OF HIS HANDS,
# HERCULES; AND HE SHOOK THE WELL-FITTED TIMBERS OF THE SHIP.
# BUT WHEN THE MYSIANS, LONGING FOR THE MAINLAND,
# THE RHYNDACIAN OUTFLOWS AND THE GREAT MOUND OF AEGAEON
# THEY MEASURED THEIR WAY PAST, BEHOLDING THEM FROM JUST BEYOND PHRYGIA.

[The Rhyndacus] is a river of Phrygia, now considered very large, flowing toward <gloss>the</gloss> east at its mouth. And [there is] the tomb of a certain Mysian hero named Aegaeon. Rhyndacus is [named] similarly to Diacos. **The great mound** <note>original: "mega ērion"</note>: This is also written as "the great headland" <note>original: "mega te rion"</note>. While a **headland** <note>term: rion; a mountain peak or promontory</note> is a mountain or cape, a **mound** <note>term: erion; a sepulchral monument or tomb</note> is a grave. I suspect that someone who did not know the myth changed the word "mound." Or, perhaps through a scribe’s error, the letter "m" was left over. The myth concerning Aegaeon is related by Demetrius of Cnidus. Conon, in his *Heracleia*, says that Aegaeon was defeated by Poseidon and buried at the place now called the "Mound of Aegaeon" by the followers of Apollonius, though he calls the same figure Briareus. Regarding the naming of the **Aegean Sea** <note>original: "Aigaion pelagos"</note>, in the third book of the *On the Islands*, it says the following: some say the Aegean Sea was named after the "Perkanian goat" <note>original: "aigos"</note>; others say it is from the woman Aegaike of Carystus. For they say that from Aegae <note>a city in Euboea</note> Poseidon comes forth. These places are in the regions around the Peloponnese. There are also some who say it is named thus because the surrounding land can be seen throughout the whole sea <note>connecting "Aigaion" to "aiges," or ripples/waves that look like goats, or perhaps a visual clarity</note>. Hesiod says that Aegaeon was the son of Uranus and Gaia <note>Heaven and Earth</note>. Briareus, Aegaeon, and Gyges are said to be the same person under different names. However, Eumelus, in his *Titanomachy*, says that Aegaeon was the child of Earth and Sea <note>original: "Pontos"</note>, and that he lives in the sea and fought as an ally to the Titans.

And Ion <note>Ion of Chios, a tragic poet and contemporary of Sophocles</note> says in a dithyramb that he [Aegaeon] was summoned from the sea by Thetis to be brought up to guard Zeus; and that he was a child of the sea. Some, however, say this was a sea monster. But Parrhasius <note>A famous Greek painter of the 5th century BCE</note> says that he was a giant who, fleeing from Euboea, arrived in Phrygia and died there. **A little way from Phrygia** <note>original: "Tyththon hyp’ ek Phrygiēs"</note>: [meaning] that which is just above Phrygia.

-> **THEN INDEED, AS HE HEAVED AGAINST THE FURROWS OF THE CHURNING SWELL,** <-
-> **HE BROKE THE OAR IN THE MIDDLE; BUT ONE FRAGMENT HE HIMSELF** <-
-> **HELD WITH BOTH HANDS AS HE FELL SIDEWAYS; THE OTHER THE SEA** <-
-> **WASHED AWAY, CARRYING IT OFF IN THE BACKWASH; AND HE SAT IN SILENCE** <-

**Heaving** <note>original: "anochlizōn"</note>: Stirring up [the water] while rowing and beating back the waves according to their flow. **Churning** <note>original: "tetrēchotos"</note>: [Meaning] the water was becoming rough and violent. **Furrows** <note>original: "holkous"</note>: The "breathings" or the risings and elevations of the waves. The phrase **from the middle** <note>original: "messothen"</note> provides an indication of both the dreadfulness of the sea and the hero’s immense strength. **Fragment** <note>original: "tryphos"</note>: The broken piece of the oar. **He broke it in the middle**: For this reason, they say, Heracles was left behind in Cios; though others say it was in Aphetae, because he made the *Argo* tilt to one side <note>His strength and weight were so great they threw the ship off balance</note>. But Ephorus <note>A prominent Greek historian of the 4th century BCE</note> records in his first book that he was left behind because of Omphale <note>The Queen of Lydia whom Heracles was forced to serve as a slave</note>. **Were unaccustomed** <note>original: "aētheson"</note>: They were unaccustomed to being at rest because of the hero’s innate power. **At the entrance** <note>original: "en promolēi"</note>: In the approach and the gateways; these outer gate areas are called **entrances** <note>term: promolai</note>, as he [Apollonius] says in the first books: "he spoke at the entrances... and those opposite were mocking." **Worn down** <note>original: "tetrymmena"</note>: Used instead of "exhausted" by the labor. **Parched** <note>original: "austaleos"</note>: One who is dry and unwashed. **Chafed** <note>original: "peritribeas"</note>: Hands very worn from the toil. The word **he prayed** <note>original: "ērēsato"</note> is used here instead of "he cursed" or "he addressed."

**Poplar** <note>original: "Aigeiros"</note> is named from its "rising from the earth" <note>original: "era"</note> and "being moved." Or perhaps because it is "broken" by the winds. **He stripped off the skin** <note>original: "elu d’ apo derma"</note>: the next part of the story says he stripped off the lion’s skin. **Bronze-heavy** <note>original: "chalkobarei"</note> refers to it being "strong," or perhaps "weighted with bronze at the end." Peisander, however, claims that the club of Heracles was made entirely of bronze. They derive the word for "club" <note>original: "rhopalon"</note> from "forceful movement" <note>original: "rhopene"</note>.

**Gies** <note>likely referring to the "earth-born" or a giant</note> is a beloved term. He compares the fir tree to the earth because it is straight-cut and lacks branches <note>original: "anauxesthe"</note>, standing like a measuring rod. The "winter season" illustrates the sudden, forceful appearance of the hero. The "violent wind" represents his strength. The phrase **with the wedges themselves** <note>original: "autoisi sphenessi"</note> refers to the piles of earth surrounding the roots of the fir; for those, too, surrounded the root in the manner of wedges. He refers to the **forestays** <note>original: "protonous"</note> to describe the tension and stretching of the roots. **Meanwhile** <note>original: "Tophra"</note> means "during the time that." **Hylas**: Apollonius says that Hylas was the son of Theiodamas. However, Hellanicus says he was the son of Theomenes. Anticleides, in his *History of Delos*, records that Hylas went out for water, but that he did not remain "undiscovered" <note>implying he was found or his fate was known</note>. There were many who were loved by Heracles: Hylas, Philoctetes, Diomus, Peirithous, and Phrix—from whom a city in Libya takes its name. Socrates <note>likely Socrates of Argos, a geographer/historian</note> says in his *Address to Eubulus* that Hylas was actually the beloved of Polyphemus, not Heracles.

Onasos, in the first book of his *Amazonides*, sets forth a more realistic version of the story, claiming that Hylas was not snatched away by nymphs, but rather that he fell into a spring and died in that manner. <note>Ancient commentators often debated whether mythological events were literal or poetic "glosses" for natural accidents.</note> It is considered unseemly for a young man to carry a water jar <note>original: "hydrian"</note>. Homer, for instance, primarily depicts young girls <note>original: "parthenon"</note> performing this task. It would be more plausible to suggest both versions, as Callimachus does. Speaking of him as a small child <note>original: "nēpiachonta"</note>, Heracles:

> Sought the sacred flow of a spring, so that water 
> might be available to him for the evening meal. But he

</margin>

...because he poured the washing water <note>original: "niptra"</note> over his hands <note>Scholars suggest Heracles was angered by a mistake in banquet etiquette or that the boy poured water intended for feet over his hands.</note>. Fleeing the murder and arriving with his wife, he killed the centaur Nessus at the Evenus river, as Archilochus also records. Then, proceeding further, he also brought Hylas, his son <note>The text here identifies Hylas as Heracles's son, though he is more commonly called his squire or ward.</note>. He came to Dryopia, a tribe of bandits bordering the Malians, as Pherecydes says in his third book. When the child was hungry and his tutor Lichas was away, Heracles met Theiodamas and asked for a little food. But he would not give it. Enraged, Heracles seized and slaughtered one of his oxen and feasted. Theiodamas then went to the city of the Dryopes and led them out against Heracles. Heracles was placed in such a desperate position that he even armed his wife Deianira. They say that she was even wounded in the breast at that time. After prevailing over them and killing Theiodamas, he took his son Hylas. The entire nation was relocated to Trachis, the Thessalian city, and Mount Oeta near the borders of Phocis, so that through the change of location and mixing with other people, they might cease their bandit-like habits. Callimachus also mentions this. Pherecydes says in his second book that the river Peneios lay with Polydora, the daughter of Danaus. From them was born Dryops, after whom the Dryopes are named. They live by the Spercheios river.

**Gadfly** <note>original: "myops"</note>: a kind of fly born during the spring which, sitting upon the eyes of oxen, bites them and drives them to madness. From this, it is also called a "sting" <note>original: "oistros"</note>. Sostratos, in his *History of Animals*, distinguishes the gadfly from the sting-fly. For the gadfly is born from wood, but the sting-fly comes from small animals floating in rivers. **Meadows** <note>original: "pisea"</note>: well-watered, marshy, and muddy places.

"Crag" <note>original: Lepas</note>: Some define this as marshy and muddy places; but it is better to understand it as rocky places, named from being "peeled" <note>original: lepesthai</note> by the sun, wind, and rain. This is also why the peaks of mountains are called "scaly" <note>original: lepre</note>. Euripides writes: "and the crag of Cithaeron." The phrase "As when [a bull] raging" makes the simile complete; for the poet compares Heracles to a wounded bull because of the hero's strength.

> AS WHEN RAGING [BY A GADFLY], NOW HE WOULD SHAKE HIS SWIFT KNEES
> CONTINUOUSLY, AND NOW AGAIN CEASING FROM HIS TOIL
> HE WOULD BELLOW A LOUD CRY PIERCING AFAR.
> IMMEDIATELY THE MORNING STAR HELD ABOVE THE HIGHEST PEAKS,
> AND THE BREEZES DESCENDED. QUICKLY THEN TIPHYS
> URGED THEM TO EMBARK AND TAKE ADVANTAGE OF THE WIND.
> THEY EMBARKED STRAIGHTWAY IN THEIR EAGERNESS. AND HIGH FROM THE SHIP,
> HAVING DRAGGED UP THE ANCHOR-STONES, THEY HAULED IN THE ROPES.
> THE SAILS WERE CURVED IN THE MIDDLE BY THE WIND. AND FAR FROM THE COAST
> THEY WERE CARRIED REJOICING PAST THE NEPTUNIAN CAPE.
> WHEN FROM HEAVEN THE BRIGHT-EYED DAWN SHINES FROM BELOW,
> RISING FROM THE EAST, AND THE PATHS SHINE THROUGH CLEARLY.

This describes the departure of Jason and the other companions. The phrase "at other times unceasing" <note>original: allot’ apaustos</note> means that sometimes he exerted himself until he was weary, and sometimes he paused. The phrase "the bellowing" <note>original: mukema</note> indicates that he, too, was shouting as he called for Hylas. "Immediately the highest [peaks]" refers to the morning star <note>the planet Venus seen before sunrise</note>. The logic of the passage is as follows: when the morning star appeared at the mountain ridges, immediately the breezes arrived. Quickly Tiphys commanded them to embark and cast off. "They hauled in" <note>original: anekrousanto</note> refers to the sequence of events; it implies they loosened the sails. "High from the ship" means they pulled up the anchors and moved the ship from its mooring. The historian Ephorus is being ridiculous when he thinks that Anacharsis <note>a famous Scythian philosopher</note> was the first to invent the double-fluked anchor; for the Argonauts lived long before Anacharsis. "When from heaven the bright-eyed" <note>original: charope</note>: he calls the dawn "bright-eyed" because it brightens and lights up the air. The terms "grayish-blue" <note>original: glaukos</note> and "bright-eyed" <note>original: charopos</note> are used as synonyms here; both refer to a quality of brilliant light. Therefore, they also used the word "shine through" <note>original: diaglausousin</note>, meaning to illuminate or flash through.

...and fought alongside him against the Amazons; he also slew Alcyoneus, as Pindar <note>A famous Greek lyric poet</note> relates. Theocritus <note>The creator of pastoral poetry</note> highlighted their friendship, saying: "The two companions always dined at one table." The meaning of the phrase "sit thou thus at ease" is "you sit there quietly as if nothing happened." Now, while Apollonius says that Heracles was left behind at Cios having gone out to search for Hylas, Dionysius of Mitylene says that the hero actually sailed with the noblemen as far as Colchis and assisted Jason in the matters regarding Medea. Demaratus says the same. However, Herodorus says he did not sail with them. Hesiod, in the *Marriage of Ceyx*, says that he went out to search for water and was left behind in Magnesia, at the place called "The Departures" <note>original: Aphetae</note> because of his dismissal there. Antimachus, in the *Lyde*, says that Heracles was put off the ship because his great weight was sinking the Argo. This version was followed by the epigrammatist Posidippus and by Pherecydes. Ephorus, in his tenth book, says he was left behind voluntarily because of Omphale, the queen of the Lydians. Uniquely, Anticlides, in the second book of his *Delian Matters*, says it was Hyllus, the son of Heracles, who went for water and did not return.

...[words like] shame <note>aischos</note>, character <note>ethos</note>, breadth <note>euros</note>, and form <note>eidos</note>; thus also pleasure <note>edos</note>. The word for "character" <note>ethos</note> is marked with a rough breathing, and this word also has a connection to the letter 'theta'; in the sense of the future "I shall please" <note>eso</note> being aspirated, though the "to thee" is omitted. For the sense is: "But what such pleasure is there to me in words?" For I shall flow <note>or "I am gone"</note> apart from those who fashioned this trick with you. "Sparks" <note>ostliges</note>: these are gleams. In other authors, the word also signifies "curls of hair," derived from "the oil flows from the burning stones." But Herodian says in the twenty-sixth book of his *General Prosody* that in Apollonius and Philetas it is spelled with an 'a', derived from "to make holy" <note>hosio</note>; by parallel. "Forcing through the gulf" <note>laitma biesamenoi</note>: instead of "fighting against the driving wind and forcing their way." "Gulf" <note>laitma</note> refers to the hollow of the sea or the distance; as if it were a "cutting" <note>latmema</note>; or from "being struck" <note>latysesthai</note> by the waves, which means to be beaten. Silenus <note>a grammarian</note> says in his *Glossary* that it means the open sea. And Hyrcanus in his first book on Apollonius [says something similar]. "If not the Thracian [sons of Boreas]": Heracles later killed these two <note>Zetes and Calais</note> when he found them at the island of Tenos or nearby. He did this out of jealousy, since Heracles bore a grudge against Boreas. Homer says: "whom you, persuading the storms with the North Wind <note>Boreas</note>..." Aenesidemus says in his *Teian History* that after they had been guests of Heracles, they laid a trap for him, wishing to murder him.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Book 1 of the Argonautica. Having just described the heated argument between Telamon and Jason over the abandonment of Heracles, the commentator now turns to the fate of the Boreads (the winged sons of the North Wind) who convinced the Argonauts to sail on without him.</meta>

"For from the games of Pelias..." <note>original: Athlon gar Peliao</note> down to the phrase "around them again," explaining that Heracles killed the Boreads because they prevented the ship from turning back to Mysia <note>the region where Heracles was left searching for Hylas</note>, according to Apollonius. However, Semus <note>a historian from Delos</note> says it was because Heracles was defeated by the Boreads in a foot-race. Skombrotos says they had a dispute with Heracles concerning the

<margin>
gifts given by Jason to the heroes <note>the "Aristeis" or best men</note>. Nicander of Colophon, in the first book of his *Oetaica*, says that Boreas <note>the North Wind, their father</note> was actually the cause of their death because he caused a storm for Heracles as he was returning from Cos.
</margin>

> **WRETCHED MEN! INDEED, A HATEFUL VENGEANCE FELL UPON THEM AFTERWARD**
> **AT THE HANDS OF HERACLES, BECAUSE THEY RESTRAINED THOSE SEEKING HIM.**
> **FOR AS THEY WERE RETURNING FROM THE GAMES OF THE DECEASED PELIAS,**
> **HE SLEW THEM IN SEA-GIRT TENOS AND HEAPED THE EARTH**
> **AROUND THEM. AND HE BUILT TWO PILLARS ABOVE THEM,**
> **OF WHICH ONE—A MARVEL BEYOND MEASURE FOR MEN TO BEHOLD—**
> **MOVES AT THE BREATH OF THE SOUNDING NORTH WIND.**
> **AND THESE THINGS WERE TO BE FULFILLED IN THE COURSE OF TIME.**
> **BUT TO THEM GLAUCUS APPEARED FROM THE DEPTHS OF THE SEA,**
> **THE WISE INTERPRETER OF DIVINE NEREUS.**

"Deceased" <note>original: Dedoupoton</note>; for after the death of Pelias <note>the king who sent Jason on the quest</note>, as the Boreads were returning to their homeland from his funeral games, Heracles happened upon them. Remembering that they had prevented the others from searching for him, he killed them on the island of Tenos. "Two pillars": <gloss>Note 3</gloss> there is a tomb in Tenos and two pillars; it happens that one of them is moved by the wind of Boreas, their father. "And these things were to be": this line is from Callimachus. It is a common error for every poet <gloss>writing</gloss> <gloss>after Homer</gloss> to express verbs starting with a consonant in the present tense by using a "k" in the imperfect tense <note>a technical grammatical point regarding the "k" augment in later Greek poetry</note>. "But to them Glaucus": Glaucus was the son of Polybus, a native of Anthedon. Anthedon is a city in Boeotia, as Homer also says: "and Anthedon at the furthest border." He was a fisherman by trade. Having once caught many fish, he was carrying them along <unclear>the road</unclear> and <unclear>at a certain spot</unclear> he set down his load of fish. When the fish ate a certain immortal herb, they came back to life. Seeing this, Glaucus also took some and ate it, and he himself was made immortal.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Book 1 of the Argonautica, following the appearance of the sea-god Glaucus. In the previous section, the commentator discussed the death of the Boreads; here, we see the prophetic speech of Glaucus as he rises from the waves to explain why Heracles and Polyphemus must be left behind.</meta>

"The deep" <note>original: brychian</note> refers to the bellowing or roaring of the sea. Then, as Glaucus reached the extreme of old age and could no longer endure its weight, he cast himself into the sea; he was thereafter honored as a sea-deity. They say the "Glaucus-fish" was named after him. By "the keel-part" <note>original: nēion meros</note>, the poet refers to the section of the ship that is dragged through the water. "Why [do you strive] against the great..." The sense of the following passage is: "Why do you rage against the will of Zeus?"

## LIFTING HIS SHAGGY HEAD AND CHEST FROM THE DEPTHS, 
## FROM HIS LOINS BELOW, HE REACHED OUT WITH A STURDY HAND 
## TO THE SHIP’S KEEL, AND CRIED OUT TO THE HASTENING HEROES:
## "WHY DO YOU STRIVE AGAINST THE WILL OF GREAT ZEUS,
## SEEKING TO BRING BOLD HERACLES TO THE CITY OF AEETES?
## IN ARGOS, IT IS HIS FATE TO SERVE THE INSOLENT EURYSTHEUS
## AND COMPLETE ALL TWELVE LABORS THROUGH MUCH TOIL.
## HE SHALL THEN DWELL AT THE HEARTH OF THE IMMORTALS, IF HE BUT
## FINISHES A FEW MORE; SO LET THERE BE NO REGRET FOR HIM.
## LIKEWISE, IT IS ORDAINED FOR POLYPHEMUS TO FOUND
## A FAMOUS CITY FOR THE MYSIANS AT THE MOUTHS OF THE CIOS
## AND FILL THE MEASURE OF HIS FATE IN THE VAST LAND OF THE CHALYBES.
## BUT HYLAS, FOR THE SAKE OF LOVE, A DIVINE NYMPH HAS MADE
## HER OWN HUSBAND—THESE THREE WERE LEFT BEHIND AS THEY WANDERED."
## HE SPOKE, AND PLUNGED BENEATH THE SURGING WAVES.
## AROUND HIM, THE FOAMING WATER SWIRLED IN EDDIES,
## DARK PURPLE, AND SWEPT THROUGH THE HOLLOW SHIP FROM THE SEA.
## THE HEROES REJOICED, AND THE SHIP SPEEDED ONWARD.

Regarding "sharing a hearth" <note>original: syndiaiton</note>, it means one who is equal in honor; because they share a common essence, they share the same honor. "At the mouths of the Cios": there is a river in Mysia from which the city Cios takes its name. For Polyphemus died fighting among the Chalybes, who are a Scythian nation. "The Chalybes": a Scythian tribe where iron is produced. There was a battle there; may the race of the Chalybes perish! <note>The commentator here echoes a common poetic sentiment against the inventors of iron weapons.</note> "Her own husband" <note>original: hon posin</note>: This is poorly written in the text. "Hon posin" is used as a possessive, meaning "her own." It should have been written "hēs posin" to make the meaning clear: that the Nymph reached out to take him as her own husband. "Plunged" <note>original: Alisason</note>: meaning he dove or went under.

<column-break/>

"The will of great Zeus": That is to say, why are you eager to go against the plan of Zeus? "In Argos it is his fate": This refers to the fact that while performing his labors, Heracles was left behind so that these others <note>the Argonauts</note> could set out toward the best of men. Apollonius himself says this in the "Catalog of Heroes." "If he still finishes a few": If he completes a few more toils—that is, if he finishes his labors—he will be with the gods.

<vocab>
**Heracles:** The famous Greek hero known for his strength and twelve labors.
**Will of Zeus:** The divine plan or destiny ordained by the king of the gods.
**Aeetes:** The king of Colchis and keeper of the Golden Fleece.
**Argos:** The region in Greece where Heracles was forced to serve King Eurystheus.
**Eurystheus:** The king who commanded Heracles to perform his famous labors.
**Polyphemus:** Not the Cyclops, but an Argonaut and hero of the Lapiths.
**Chalybes:** A legendary tribe of iron-smiths living on the south coast of the Black Sea.
**Nymph:** A nature spirit; here, one who fell in love with Heracles' squire, Hylas.
**Apollonius:** The author of the *Argonautica* (3rd century BCE).
</vocab>

Thoughtfully; with deliberation and intelligence. "But to the winds let us give [the error]"; the meaning in the poet is: deeds that are unstable and fleeting, let the storms snatch them away and carry them off at once. You reviled; you insulted. For the word "glory" <note>original: kydos</note> in the masculine gender means "insult" among the people of Syracuse. Sophocles uses it this way in *Ajax the Whip-Bearer*: "he is insulted <note>original: kydazetai</note> by all the Greeks together." "Of a kind man"; the grammatical cases are swapped <note>A technical note on a poetic shift from the expected genitive to another case</note>; for the sense is that it is <unclear>fitting</unclear> for a man to err. Being reconciled; having become friends. "Eponymous"; instead of "having the same name as the river." For the city was named Cios, also called <unclear>Ciamus</unclear>, because <unclear>Ciamus</unclear> founded it after leading the colony there.

<note>This poetic section summarizes how Heracles forced the Mysians to continue the search for his lost squire, Hylas, by taking their children as hostages and relocating them to Trachis.</note>

...of the god Ilaios. **Whether living they might find the fate of Hylas.** The word "fate" <note>original: moron</note> should be understood as "portion" or "destiny" <note>original: moiran</note>. For the name is derived from "portion," just as in Homer, "at Pylos among the dead." "Fate," therefore, refers to the destiny of one living or dead, or the final state of their destiny, whether they are alive or a corpse. **And as pledges for him they gave.** Instead of Hylas, the Mysians provided <term>pledges</term> <note>original: rhysia; specifically legal seizures or hostages given as security</note> to Heracles in exchange for his constant searching. The preposition "from" <note>original: apo</note> is redundant here. **Searching.** Meaning "seeking," from which we also get "investigation" <note>original: mastikē</note>. Callimachus says: "I grew weary searching." From this, breasts <note>original: mastoi</note> are also so named because they are necessarily sought by infants <note>This is an example of ancient folk etymology, linking the Greek words for 'seeking' and 'breasts'</note>. **They will seek.** Used instead of "they investigate" or "they look for." Homer says: "Searching for these, he met with pain," and "he searches the mountain glens." **And they care for well-built Trachis.** Trachis is a city in Thessaly where Heracles settled the children of the Mysians when he received them as <term>pledges</term> for Hylas. "Right there" <note>original: autothi</note> is used to mean "in that very place." It indicates the present location, equal to staying "on the spot," as in "lest we somehow miss each other." **Pledges** <note>original: Rhysia</note>: These are things given as security or hostages in exchange for someone’s release. It is said that the Cians <note>the inhabitants of the city of Cius in Mysia</note> gave hostages to Heracles and swore that they would never cease their labor in searching for Hylas. They still maintain a concern for the people of Trachis <note>original: rhachiniōn</note> because those who were taken as hostages were settled there by Heracles. Cinaethon records this history in his work *The Heracleia*.

**"Now all day"** <note>original: Nyn de panēmeriēn</note>: The meaning is as follows: throughout the entire day and night, the wind carried the ship, blowing with great force. But when the day appeared...

<margin>
...the wind had ceased slightly before. **Protruding** <note>original: Eisamechousan</note>: this means standing out or being extended. Or, seeing a **level shore** <note>original: amechousan aktēn</note> that was flattened and sloping, they became oarsmen and brought the ship to its mooring.
</margin>
