<meta>This page continues the story of Euphemus and the divine clod of earth given to him by the sea-god Triton. The narrative moves from Euphemus's prophetic dream to the actual founding of the island of Thera (modern-day Santorini) and the eventual colonization of Cyrene in Libya. The text includes both the primary poetic verses of Apollonius of Rhodes and the scholarly commentary (scholia) that explains the historical and mythological context.</meta>

And according to **Akesander** <note>A lost 3rd-century BC historian who wrote about the history of Cyrene</note> in his first book on **Cyrene**; he discusses the "prey" <note>original: *thēra*, a pun on the name of the island Thera</note>: how the island was created from the clod of earth thrown there, appearing at **Aegile** and rising up in the sea. **Pindar** <note>The famous lyric poet</note> says that the clod melted and flowed away around the island now called **Thera**, because the servants failed to hold onto it; but **Apollonius** says that **Euphemus** <note>The Argonaut with the power to walk on water</note> 

voluntarily threw the clod into the sea, following the advice of **Jason**. It was originally called the island of **Kalliste**; it received this name because it was "the most beautiful" <note>original: *kallistē*</note> island. Later it was named **Thera**, after **Theras**, the son of **Autesion**. He led a colony there from **Sparta** after they were driven out of **Lemnos**—

<column-break/>

"O SONS! SINCE **TRITON** <note>The sea-god, son of Poseidon</note> GRANTED THIS GUEST-GIFT TO YOU FROM THE **LIBYAN CONTINENT**; FOR NO OTHER IMMORTAL GAVE IT TO HIM SAVE HE WHO ENCOUNTERED HIM. SO HE SPOKE; AND **EUPHEMUS** DID NOT MAKE LIGHT OF THE RESPONSE OF THE **SON OF AESON** <note>Jason</note>; REJOICING AT THE DIVINE PROPHECIES, HE CAST THE CLOD INTO THE DEPTHS. AND FROM IT AN ISLAND ROSE UP, THE **MOST BEAUTIFUL**, THE SACRED NURSE OF THE CHILDREN OF **EUPHEMUS**. THEY PREVIOUSLY DWELT ON **SINTIAN LEMNOS**; BUT DRIVEN OUT OF **LEMNOS** BY **TYRRHENIAN** MEN <note>Often identified with the Pelasgians or early Etruscans</note>, THEY REACHED **SPARTA** AS REFUGEES. AND WHEN THEY LEFT **SPARTA**, THE NOBLE SON OF **AUTESION**, **THERAS**, LED THEM TO THE MOST BEAUTIFUL ISLAND; HE CHANGED THE NAME TO **THERA** AFTER HIMSELF. BUT THESE EVENTS OCCURRED LATER THAN **EUPHEMUS**. FROM THERE, LEAVING THE HARBOR OF **ASTERIOS** THROUGH THE VAST SWELL, THEY HELD THEIR COURSE TO THE SHORES OF **AEGINA**; AND IMMEDIATELY THEY ENGAGED IN A BLAMELESS CONTEST CONCERNING WATER-FETCHING, TO SEE WHO, AFTER DRAWING THE WATER, MIGHT REACH THE SHIP FIRST."

---

—having been driven out by the **Tyrrhenians**, they went to **Sparta** as settlers. One descendant born from **Euphemus** was himself called **Aristotle** <note>Also known as Battus, the first king of Cyrene. The commentator identifies the philosopher's namesake with the colonizer</note>, and he led the colony to **Libya**. **Theras** had his lineage from **Oedipus** <note>The tragic King of Thebes</note>; for he was the son of **Autesion**, son of **Tisamenus**, son of **Thersander**, son of **Polynices**, son of **Oedipus**. The **Lemnians**, who had been cast out by the **Tyrrhenians** from **Lemnos**, also followed **Theras** to **Africa**. <term>Asperōs</term>: Most quickly. <term>Hydreian</term>: The act of fetching water. <term>Phthaiē</term>: Should arrive first; clearly, whoever might first take the water.

<summary>This page describes the mythological origin of the island of Thera (Santorini) from a divine clod of earth and recounts the lineage of its colonizers, tracing them back to the Argonaut Euphemus and the house of Oedipus.</summary>
<keywords>Euphemus, Thera, Kalliste, Jason, Triton, Cyrene, Lemnos, Sparta, Theras, colonization, divine clod, Aegina</keywords>

--- Page 347 ---
<meta>This page concludes the final book (Book IV) of Apollonius Rhodius's epic poem, the *Argonautica*. It follows the Argonauts as they leave the island of Aegina and complete their long journey home to Pagasae. The text marks the end of the poem and includes the printer's colophon for this 1496 Florence edition.</meta>

<margin>
Since now for you the struggle [has ended]: because no other contest or trial befell you after departing from **Aegina** until you returned; neither did violent winds arise or set in; instead, you sailed calmly past both **Attica** and **Aulid**; **Euboea** and the cities of the **Locrians**. Gracious and in good calm, you entered into the harbors of all [the cities]; from where you had also sailed away together toward **Scythia** <note>The region at the eastern edge of the Black Sea</note> for the sake of the **Golden Fleece**. 

**Whirlwinds** <note>original: *Eriolai*</note>: the gusts and rotations of great winds. 

**Aulis** is a city of **Boeotia**...
</margin>

FOR BOTH NECESSITY AND A BOUNDLESS RACE URGED THEM ON;
WHERE STILL NOW, FILLING THEIR AMPHORAS ON THEIR SHOULDERS,
TAKING THEM UP WITH LIGHT FEET IMMEDIATELY IN THE CONTEST,
THE YOUNG MEN OF THE **MYRMIDONS** <note>The people of Aegina, famously transformed from ants by Zeus</note> STRIVE FOR VICTORY.
BE PROPITIOUS, RACE OF BLESSED NOBLES; AND MAY THESE SONGS
BE SWEETER TO SING FROM YEAR TO YEAR
FOR MEN; FOR NOW I HAVE REACHED THE GLORIOUS ENDS
OF YOUR LABORS; SINCE NO FURTHER STRUGGLE BEFELL YOU
AS YOU RETURNED HOMEWARD FROM **AEGINA**;
NOR DID THE WHIRLWINDS <note>original: *eriolai*</note> OF WINDS ARISE; BUT PEACEFULLY
MEASURING THE **CECROPIAN LAND** <note>original: *Kekropian*, a poetic name for Athens/Attica after king Cecrops</note> AND PAST **AULIS**
WITHIN **EUBOEA**; AND THE **OPUNTIAN CITIES** OF THE **LOCRIANS**.
JOYFULLY YOU STEPPED UPON THE **PAGASAEAN SHORES** <note>The starting point of the expedition in Thessaly</note>.

<margin>
...lying opposite **Euboea**. **Opuntian cities**: those once held by **Opus**, the son of **Zeus** and **Protogeneia**; for whom the city is named; **Opus** is also a river of **Locris**. **Joyfully upon the Pagasaean shores**: you entered into the beaches of **Pagasae**; from where you also sailed away at the beginning.
</margin>

# ->THE END OF APOLLONIUS'<-
